  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

anihpj's 4 C's — Applied to Our Platform

💻
CODE Layer — anihpj/jobpost

bandit SAST scans Django code for SQL injection, XSS, hardcoded secrets. safety checks requirements.txt for known CVEs. git-secrets prevents committing AWS keys. All run in CI before any build.

📦
CONTAINER Layer — Docker Image

Trivy scans the built image for OS and language CVEs. Cosign signs the image with keyless Sigstore. Image runs as UID 1000, read-only root FS. Base image: python:3.12-slim (minimal attack surface).

☸️
CLUSTER Layer — Kubernetes

RBAC: anihpj-devs Role scoped to dev namespace. PSA Restricted on all app namespaces. NetworkPolicies: default-deny, only allowed paths open. Kyverno: validates, mutates, verifies images.

☁️
CLOUD Layer — AWS

IAM Roles for EC2 nodes (not admin!). VPC with private subnets for worker nodes. KMS encrypts EBS volumes and S3. CloudTrail logs all API calls. Security groups restrict node ports.

How the 4 C's Defend Against a Real Attack — A Walkthrough

Let's trace an attacker trying to compromise anihpj. At each layer, they encounter a defense. This is why defense-in-depth matters — NO single layer is sufficient:

1
Attacker finds a SQL injection in anihpj/jobpost (Code Layer)

Defense: SAST (bandit). If bandit was run in CI, this SQL injection would have been caught at PR review — before ever reaching production. If bandit was skipped → attacker proceeds to exploit the running application.

2
Attacker gains shell inside the container (Container Layer)

Defense: Security Context. runAsNonRoot: true → attacker is UID 1000, not root. readOnlyRootFilesystem: true → attacker can't write malware to disk. capabilities.drop: [ALL] → attacker can't escalate privileges. Seccomp blocks dangerous syscalls. The attacker is CONTAINED.

3
Attacker tries to access the database (Cluster Layer)

Defense: NetworkPolicy. Only anihpj-api pod can reach the DB on port 5432. The compromised pod (anihpj-web) can't even SEE the database. RBAC limits the pod's ServiceAccount to read one Secret — not list all Secrets. The attacker is ISOLATED.

4
Attacker tries to access cloud resources (Cloud Layer)

Defense: IAM + VPC. The node's IAM role is scoped to ECR pull only. No S3, no DynamoDB, no admin. The node is in a private subnet — no direct internet access. CloudTrail logs every API call. The attacker is BLOCKED at the cloud boundary.

💡 The lesson: If ANY of these layers were missing, the attacker would have succeeded. Code layer missed the SQLi → Container layer contained the breach. Container layer missed the privilege escalation → Cluster layer isolated the pod. This is defense-in-depth in action.

10.2 Authentication, Authorization & Admission (AAA) — The Request Pipeline

Every kubectl command travels through THREE security gates before reaching etcd. Understanding the AAA flow is essential for debugging "Forbidden" errors and designing platform access controls:

AAA FLOW — Every API Request Goes Through This
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                 │
  │  $ kubectl create deploy anihpj-api --image=anihpj:v2.1         │
  │       │                                                         │
  │  ┌────▼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │  GATE 1: AUTHENTICATION (AuthN) — "WHO are you?"         │  │
  │  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │  │
  │  │  │ Methods:                                            │  │  │
  │  │  │ • X.509 Client Certificate (kubeconfig)             │  │  │
  │  │  │ • Bearer Token (ServiceAccount JWT)                 │  │  │
  │  │  │ • OIDC Token (human user via Google/GitHub)         │  │  │
  │  │  │ • Webhook Token (external auth service)             │  │  │
  │  │  │                                                     │  │  │
  │  │  │ → Result: "user=alice, groups=platform-team"        │  │  │
  │  │  │ → FAIL? → HTTP 401 Unauthorized                     │  │  │
  │  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │  │
  │  └────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                           │ PASS                                 │
  │  ┌────────────────────────▼────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │  GATE 2: AUTHORIZATION (AuthZ) — "WHAT can you do?"        │  │
  │  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │  │
  │  │  │ • RBAC: Role → RoleBinding → User/Group/SA          │  │  │
  │  │  │ • Node: kubelet authorization                       │  │  │
  │  │  │ • ABAC: Attribute-based (legacy, avoid)             │  │  │
  │  │  │ • Webhook: External authorization (OPA, custom)     │  │  │
  │  │  │                                                     │  │  │
  │  │  │ Check: Can alice CREATE deployments in anihpj-dev?  │  │  │
  │  │  │ → RBAC lookup: Role "anihpj-dev-role" ✓             │  │  │
  │  │  │ → FAIL? → HTTP 403 Forbidden                        │  │  │
  │  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │  │
  │  └────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                           │ PASS                                 │
  │  ┌────────────────────────▼────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │  GATE 3: ADMISSION CONTROL — "SHOULD we allow this?"       │  │
  │  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │  │
  │  │  │ a. Mutating Webhooks (modify object):               │  │  │
  │  │  │    • Kyverno: add default resource limits           │  │  │
  │  │  │    • Istio: inject Envoy sidecar                    │  │  │
  │  │  │                                                     │  │  │
  │  │  │ b. Validating Webhooks (accept/reject):             │  │  │
  │  │  │    • Kyverno: check limits, probes, image source    │  │  │
  │  │  │    • PSA: check pod security context                │  │  │
  │  │  │    • Gatekeeper: evaluate Rego policies             │  │  │
  │  │  │                                                     │  │  │
  │  │  │ → FAIL? → "admission webhook denied: [reason]"      │  │  │
  │  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │  │
  │  └────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                           │ PASS                                 │
  │                    ┌──────▼──────┐                               │
  │                    │ ✅ PERSIST  │  Object stored in etcd         │
  │                    └─────────────┘                               │
  │                                                                 │
  │  💡 DEBUGGING QUICK REFERENCE:                                   │
  │     "401 Unauthorized" → AuthN failed (bad cert/token)           │
  │     "403 Forbidden"    → AuthZ failed (RBAC doesn't allow)       │
  │     "admission webhook denied" → Admission failed (policy)       │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Authentication Methods — How Kubernetes Knows WHO You Are

The CNPA exam expects you to understand multiple authentication methods, when to use each, and how they integrate. Kubernetes itself does NOT store users — it delegates authentication to external systems. Here's a deep dive into every method:

MethodHow It WorksBest ForCNPA Note
X.509 Client Certificateskubeconfig contains a client cert signed by the cluster CA. API server extracts username from the certificate's Common Name (CN) and groups from Organization (O) fields.
openssl req -subj "/CN=alice/O=platform-team"		Kubernetes components (kubelet, scheduler), service accounts, legacy setupsHard to revoke (requires CRL or API server restart). Moving to OIDC for humans.
Bearer Tokens (ServiceAccount)Pods authenticate using a JWT mounted at /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token. Token is a signed JWT containing the SA name and namespace.Pods authenticating to the K8s API. Every pod gets this automatically.Tokens are short-lived (1 hour) in K8s 1.22+. Old non-expiring tokens were a security risk.
OpenID Connect (OIDC)Human logs in via identity provider (Google, GitHub, Azure AD). IdP issues an ID token. kubectl sends this token to API server. API server validates the JWT signature against the IdP's public keys.Human users. The CNPA-recommended method for people.Requires configuring OIDC flags on kube-apiserver. Enables SSO, MFA, and centralized user management.
Webhook Token AuthenticationAPI server sends the bearer token to an external webhook service. Webhook returns user identity (username, groups, UID) or denies. The webhook can be anything — LDAP lookup, custom logic, OPA policy.Custom authentication logic. Legacy LDAP integration. Temporary access tokens.Webhook must be highly available — if it's down, NO ONE can authenticate. Use with caution.
Service Account Token Volume ProjectionK8s 1.22+ uses the TokenRequest API to generate short-lived, audience-bound, time-bound tokens. Token is projected as a file in the pod (not a Secret). Token auto-refreshes via kubelet.ALL pod-to-API-server communication. The modern standard.Replaces old Secret-based tokens. Tokens are pod-UID-bound — stolen token can't be reused from another pod.

Configuring OIDC on kube-apiserver — The CNPA Setup

OIDC configuration happens via kube-apiserver flags. This is how you enable human users to authenticate with their corporate identity provider:

kube-apiserver OIDC Configuration 
# /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - kube-apiserver
    # ─── OIDC Configuration ───
    - --oidc-issuer-url=https://accounts.google.com
    # Where to validate ID tokens (must be HTTPS)

    - --oidc-client-id=1234567890-abc.apps.googleusercontent.com
    # The OAuth2 client ID registered with the IdP

    - --oidc-username-claim=email
    # Which JWT claim contains the username (email, sub, name)

    - --oidc-groups-claim=groups
    # Which JWT claim contains group memberships (for RBAC)

    - --oidc-ca-file=/etc/kubernetes/oidc-ca.crt
    # CA certificate for the OIDC issuer (if not publicly trusted)

    # ─── RESULT ───
    # kubectl --token=$(gcloud auth print-identity-token) get pods
    # → API server validates JWT against Google's public keys
    # → Extracts username=alice@anihpj.com, groups=["platform-team"]
    # → RBAC uses these for authorization
    # → No local users to manage. No certs to rotate. SSO + MFA built-in.

10.3 RBAC — Role-Based Access Control

RBAC is how Kubernetes answers "What can this user do?" It has four objects — two for defining permissions, two for assigning them. Mastering RBAC is essential for the CNPA exam and real-world platform administration:

The Four RBAC Objects

RBAC — The Four Objects
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                 │
  │  ┌──────────────────────┐        ┌──────────────────────┐      │
  │  │       ROLE            │        │     CLUSTERROLE       │      │
  │  │  (Namespace-scoped)   │        │   (Cluster-wide)      │      │
  │  │                      │        │                      │      │
  │  │  rules:              │        │  rules:              │      │
  │  │  - apiGroups: [""]   │        │  - apiGroups: [""]   │      │
  │  │    resources: [pods] │        │    resources: [nodes]│      │
  │  │    verbs: [get,list] │        │    verbs: [get,list] │      │
  │  │                      │        │                      │      │
  │  │  Scope: ONE namespace│        │  Scope: ALL namespaces│      │
  │  └──────────┬───────────┘        └──────────┬───────────┘      │
  │             │                               │                   │
  │             ▼                               ▼                   │
  │  ┌──────────────────────┐        ┌──────────────────────┐      │
  │  │    ROLEBINDING        │        │  CLUSTERROLEBINDING   │      │
  │  │  (Namespace-scoped)   │        │   (Cluster-wide)      │      │
  │  │                      │        │                      │      │
  │  │  roleRef:            │        │  roleRef:            │      │
  │  │    name: dev-role    │        │    name: node-reader  │      │
  │  │  subjects:           │        │  subjects:           │      │
  │  │  - kind: Group       │        │  - kind: Group       │      │
  │  │    name: anihpj-devs │        │    name: platform-team│      │
  │  │    apiGroup: rbac    │        │    apiGroup: rbac    │      │
  │  │                      │        │                      │      │
  │  │  Scope: ONE namespace│        │  Scope: ENTIRE cluster│      │
  │  └──────────────────────┘        └──────────────────────┘      │
  │                                                                 │
  │  💡 WHY FOUR OBJECTS? Role/ClusterRole = WHAT permissions.      │
  │     RoleBinding/ClusterRoleBinding = WHO gets them. Separation  │
  │     of concerns: define permissions ONCE (Role), assign MULTIPLE │
  │     times (RoleBindings in different namespaces).               │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

anihpj RBAC in Practice — Three Teams, Three Roles

anihpj-rbac.yaml — Roles + RoleBindings for Platform Teams 
# ─── ROLE 1: anihpj-dev-role (Namespace: anihpj-dev) ───
# Developers can manage their apps but NOT touch RBAC, secrets, or nodes
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: anihpj-dev-role
  namespace: anihpj-dev
rules:
- apiGroups: ["", "apps", "batch"]
  resources: ["pods", "deployments", "services", "configmaps", "jobs"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch", "create", "update", "patch", "delete"]
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["pods/log", "pods/exec"]
  verbs: ["get", "create"]    # Can view logs and exec into pods

---
# ─── ROLEBINDING 1: Bind dev-role to anihpj-developers group ───
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: anihpj-dev-binding
  namespace: anihpj-dev
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: Role
  name: anihpj-dev-role
subjects:
- kind: Group
  name: anihpj-developers
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io

---
# ─── ROLE 2: anihpj-viewer-role (Read-only across ALL namespaces) ───
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRole
metadata:
  name: anihpj-viewer
rules:
- apiGroups: ["", "apps"]
  resources: ["pods", "deployments", "services", "configmaps"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]    # READ-ONLY — no create/update/delete

---
# ─── CLUSTERROLEBINDING: Bind viewer to auditors group ───
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRoleBinding
metadata:
  name: anihpj-viewer-binding
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: anihpj-viewer
subjects:
- kind: Group
  name: anihpj-auditors
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io

# ─── RESULT ───
# anihpj-developers → can CRUD apps in anihpj-dev ONLY
# anihpj-auditors   → can VIEW pods/deploys in ALL namespaces
# Both follow LEAST PRIVILEGE principle

RBAC Debugging — "Why Can't I Create This Pod?"

🔍
kubectl auth can-i

The essential RBAC debugging tool: kubectl auth can-i create deployments --as alice -n anihpj-dev. Returns yes or no. Add --list to see ALL permissions.

📋
kubectl describe rolebinding

Shows which subjects are bound to which role: kubectl describe rolebinding -n anihpj-dev. Verify the binding exists and references the correct subjects.

⚠️
Common RBAC Mistakes

1) Using Role for cluster-scoped resources (nodes, PVs) — must use ClusterRole. 2) RoleBinding in wrong namespace. 3) Forgetting apiGroups: [""] for core, ["apps"] for deployments. 4) RoleBinding references Role from different namespace — not allowed!

✅
Least Privilege Pattern

Start with NOTHING. Add permissions one by one as developers request them. Document WHY each permission was granted. Review RBAC quarterly: kubectl get rolebindings,clusterrolebindings -A.

The RBAC Mental Model — How Kubernetes "Thinks" About Permissions

RBAC isn't just a set of YAML files — it's a specific way of thinking about access control. Understanding this mental model prevents the most common RBAC mistakes:

RBAC MENTAL MODEL — The Decision Algorithm
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                 │
  │  API Request: "alice wants to CREATE a Deployment in anihpj-dev"│
  │       │                                                         │
  │  ┌────▼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │  STEP 1: Find ALL RoleBindings in namespace anihpj-dev    │  │
  │  │  (and ALL ClusterRoleBindings — cluster-wide)             │  │
  │  └────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                           │                                      │
  │  ┌────────────────────────▼────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │  STEP 2: Filter to RoleBindings where alice is a SUBJECT    │  │
  │  │  (alice's user, groups, or ServiceAccount)                  │  │
  │  └────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                           │                                      │
  │  ┌────────────────────────▼────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │  STEP 3: Look up each binding's roleRef → Role/ClusterRole  │  │
  │  │  Get the RULES from each Role                               │  │
  │  └────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                           │                                      │
  │  ┌────────────────────────▼────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │  STEP 4: Check if ANY rule allows "create Deployment"       │  │
  │  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │  │
  │  │  │ Rules checked (OR logic — ANY match = ALLOW):        │  │  │
  │  │  │                                                      │  │  │
  │  │  │ Rule 1: apiGroups=["apps"], resources=["deployments"],│  │  │
  │  │  │         verbs=["get","list","watch"]                  │  │  │
  │  │  │         → "create" NOT in verbs → NO MATCH            │  │  │
  │  │  │                                                      │  │  │
  │  │  │ Rule 2: apiGroups=["apps"], resources=["deployments"],│  │  │
  │  │  │         verbs=["create","update","patch","delete"],   │  │  │
  │  │  │         resourceNames=["anihpj-api"]                  │  │  │
  │  │  │         → "create" IS in verbs BUT alice is creating  │  │  │
  │  │  │           "anihpj-web", not "anihpj-api"              │  │  │
  │  │  │         → resourceNames doesn't match → NO MATCH      │  │  │
  │  │  │                                                      │  │  │
  │  │  │ Rule 3: apiGroups=["apps"], resources=["deployments"],│  │  │
  │  │  │         verbs=["get","list","create","update","delete"]│  │  │
  │  │  │         → "create" IS in verbs                        │  │  │
  │  │  │         → No resourceNames filter → ALL deploys match │  │  │
  │  │  │         → MATCH! ✅                                     │  │  │
  │  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │  │
  │  └────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                           │                                      │
  │                    ┌──────▼──────┐                               │
  │                    │  ✅ ALLOW   │  "alice can create anihpj-web"│
  │                    └─────────────┘                               │
  │                                                                 │
  │  💡 KEY INSIGHTS FROM THE MENTAL MODEL:                          │
  │  • RBAC is ALLOW-ONLY — there is no "deny" rule. If no rule     │
  │    matches, the request is denied by default.                    │
  │  • Rules within a Role are OR-ed (any match = allow).           │
  │  • Roles are UNION-ed across all bindings for a subject.        │
  │  • resourceNames acts as an AND filter on top of the rule.      │
  │  • There is NO way to say "allow everything EXCEPT X."          │
  │    You must enumerate what IS allowed. This is by design.       │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

RBAC Anti-Patterns — Common Mistakes That Create Security Holes

🚫
The "cluster-admin" Default

"Just give them cluster-admin, we'll lock it down later." Later never comes. Start with NOTHING. Add permissions one by one as needed. kubectl auth can-i --list --as <user> shows exactly what they have.

🚫
RoleBinding in Wrong Namespace

Created a Role in "anihpj-dev" but the RoleBinding is in "default." Result: binding references a Role that doesn't exist in that namespace — silently broken. Always verify: kubectl describe rolebinding -n <ns>.

🚫
Using verbs: ["*"]

"Just give them all verbs, it's easier." * includes "escalate" and "bind" — which let users grant themselves MORE permissions. This is how privilege escalation happens. Always enumerate specific verbs: get, list, watch, create, update, patch, delete.

🚫
Forgetting apiGroups

apiGroups: [""] means the CORE API group (pods, services). apiGroups: ["apps"] means the APPS group (deployments, statefulsets). Missing or wrong apiGroups is the #1 reason "kubectl auth can-i says yes but kubectl says no."

RBAC AggregationRule — Composing ClusterRoles

AggregationRule lets you COMBINE multiple ClusterRoles into one. When you label a ClusterRole, all rules from ClusterRoles with matching labels are MERGED into it. This is how Kubernetes builds the built-in admin, edit, and view ClusterRoles:

RBAC AggregationRule — Composing Roles 
# ─── ClusterRole "anihpj-platform-admin" aggregates other roles ───
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRole
metadata:
  name: anihpj-platform-admin
  labels:
    rbac.anihpj.com/aggregate-to-admin: "true"
aggregationRule:
  clusterRoleSelectors:
  - matchLabels:
      rbac.anihpj.com/aggregate-to-admin: "true"
# This ClusterRole now INCLUDES all rules from EVERY ClusterRole
# that has the label rbac.anihpj.com/aggregate-to-admin: "true"
# 
# You can create separate ClusterRoles for different concerns:
#   anihpj-app-admin: CRUD on deployments, pods, services
#   anihpj-secret-admin: read secrets
#   anihpj-config-admin: manage configmaps
# Each with the label → all aggregated into platform-admin

# 💡 WHY THIS MATTERS:
# - Built-in "admin" ClusterRole uses AggregationRule
# - CRD controllers (cert-manager, Kyverno) auto-create ClusterRoles
#   for their CRDs — aggregation picks them up automatically
# - No need to manually maintain a giant ClusterRole with all rules

10.4 ServiceAccounts — Identity for Pods

ServiceAccounts provide identity for PODS (not humans). Every pod runs with a ServiceAccount, and every namespace has a default ServiceAccount. The CNPA principle: never use the default SA for application pods — always create dedicated, least-privilege SAs:

SERVICE ACCOUNT — Pod Identity Architecture
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                 │
  │  Namespace: anihpj-prod                                         │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │  ┌─────────────────────────┐   ┌───────────────────────┐ │ │
  │  │  │ ServiceAccount:         │   │ Role: db-secret-reader│ │ │
  │  │  │ anihpj-api-sa           │◀──│                       │ │ │
  │  │  │                         │   │ rules:                │ │ │
  │  │  │ automountServiceAccount │   │ - apiGroups: [""]     │ │ │
  │  │  │   Token: true           │   │   resources: [secrets]│ │ │
  │  │  └───────────┬─────────────┘   │   resourceNames:      │ │ │
  │  │              │                  │     [db-credentials]  │ │ │
  │  │              │ RoleBinding      │   verbs: [get]        │ │ │
  │  │              └──────────────────┤                       │ │ │
  │  │                                 └───────────────────────┘ │ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ │
  │  │  │ Pod: anihpj-api-7d4f8                               │ │ │
  │  │  │   serviceAccountName: anihpj-api-sa                  │ │ │
  │  │  │                                                     │ │ │
  │  │  │   /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/    │ │ │
  │  │  │     ├── token       ← Short-lived JWT (1 hour)      │ │ │
  │  │  │     ├── ca.crt      ← API server CA certificate     │ │ │
  │  │  │     └── namespace   ← Namespace name                │ │ │
  │  │  │                                                     │ │ │
  │  │  │   Python code in pod:                               │ │ │
  │  │  │   with open('/var/run/secrets/.../token') as f:     │ │ │
  │  │  │       token = f.read()                              │ │ │
  │  │  │   # Use token to authenticate to K8s API            │ │ │
  │  │  │   # Can ONLY read secret "db-credentials" ✅         │ │ │
  │  │  │   # Cannot list pods, delete deploys, or read other │ │ │
  │  │  │   # secrets ❌ (blocked by RBAC)                     │ │ │
  │  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                 │
  │  💡 LEAST PRIVILEGE CHECKLIST:                                   │
  │     ✅ Dedicated SA per application (not default)                │
  │     ✅ Role scoped to EXACT resources needed (not *)             │
  │     ✅ Token projection (short-lived, auto-rotated)              │
  │     ❌ Default SA with cluster-admin — NEVER!                    │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

anihpj ServiceAccount — Least Privilege in Practice

anihpj-api-sa.yaml — Dedicated ServiceAccount + Token Projection 
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: anihpj-api-sa
  namespace: anihpj-prod
# Token is auto-created as a Secret (or projected via TokenRequest API)

---
# Pod using the dedicated SA
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: anihpj-api
spec:
  serviceAccountName: anihpj-api-sa    # NOT "default"!
  automountServiceAccountToken: true   # Mount token at /var/run/secrets/...
  containers:
  - name: api
    image: registry.anihpj.com/jobpost:v2.1

# 💡 TOKEN PROJECTION (K8s 1.22+):
# Tokens are now SHORT-LIVED (default 1 hour) and BOUND to a specific
# pod. Even if stolen, they expire quickly and can't be reused from
# another pod. This replaces the old non-expiring Secret-based tokens.

TokenRequest API — How Short-Lived Tokens Actually Work

The TokenRequest API (K8s 1.22+) fundamentally changed how pods authenticate. Understanding this mechanism is critical because the CNPA exam tests the difference between old Secret-based tokens and new projected tokens:

TOKEN REQUEST API — Short-Lived, Pod-Bound Tokens
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                 │
  │  THE OLD WAY (pre-1.22) — Secret-Based Tokens                   │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │  1. SA created → Token stored as K8s Secret (non-expiring)│ │
  │  │  2. Pod mounts Secret as volume                            │ │
  │  │  3. Token is valid FOREVER (until SA deleted)              │ │
  │  │  4. Token is NOT bound to any specific pod                 │ │
  │  │  5. If token leaks → attacker has PERMANENT access         │ │
  │  │  6. No audience restriction — token works for any API      │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                 │
  │  THE NEW WAY (1.22+) — TokenRequest API                         │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │  Pod created with SA "anihpj-api-sa"                      │ │
  │  │       │                                                    │ │
  │  │  ┌────▼────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │ │
  │  │  │ KUBELET (on the node)                                │  │ │
  │  │  │                                                      │  │ │
  │  │  │ 1. Kubelet calls TokenRequest API:                   │  │ │
  │  │  │    POST /api/v1/namespaces/anihpj-prod/              │  │ │
  │  │  │         serviceaccounts/anihpj-api-sa/token          │  │ │
  │  │  │                                                      │  │ │
  │  │  │ 2. Request body specifies:                           │  │ │
  │  │  │    {                                                  │  │ │
  │  │  │      "audiences": ["kubernetes.default.svc"],        │  │ │
  │  │  │      "expirationSeconds": 3600   // 1 hour           │  │ │
  │  │  │    }                                                  │  │ │
  │  │  │                                                      │  │ │
  │  │  │ 3. API server generates JWT:                         │  │ │
  │  │  │    {                                                  │  │ │
  │  │  │      "sub": "system:serviceaccount:anihpj-prod:      │  │ │
  │  │  │              anihpj-api-sa",                          │  │ │
  │  │  │      "kubernetes.io": {                               │  │ │
  │  │  │        "namespace": "anihpj-prod",                    │  │ │
  │  │  │        "pod": {"uid": "a1b2c3d4-..."},  ← POD-BOUND! │  │ │
  │  │  │        "serviceaccount": {"uid": "e5f6g7h8-..."}     │  │ │
  │  │  │      },                                               │  │ │
  │  │  │      "aud": ["kubernetes.default.svc"],               │  │ │
  │  │  │      "exp": 1719000000               // 1 hour from now│  │ │
  │  │  │    }                                                  │  │ │
  │  │  │                                                      │  │ │
  │  │  │ 4. Kubelet projects token as FILE (not Secret!):      │  │ │
  │  │  │    /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/    │  │ │
  │  │  │      └── token  ← auto-refreshed by kubelet          │  │ │
  │  │  │                                                      │  │ │
  │  │  │ 5. Kubelet RE-REQUESTS a new token BEFORE expiry     │  │ │
  │  │  │    (at 80% of TTL). Pod always has a valid token.    │  │ │
  │  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │  KEY DIFFERENCES:                                         │ │
  │  │  ✅ Token is BOUND to the pod's UID (can't be reused)     │ │
  │  │  ✅ Token is AUDIENCE-RESTRICTED (only works for K8s API) │ │
  │  │  ✅ Token is TIME-LIMITED (expires in 1 hour)             │ │
  │  │  ✅ Token is a FILE, not a Secret (no etcd storage)       │ │
  │  │  ✅ Token auto-refreshes (no pod restart needed)          │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                 │
  │  💡 CNPA INSIGHT: If the exam asks "How do pods authenticate   │
  │     securely?" — the answer is TokenRequest API with projected  │
  │     tokens. "ServiceAccount Secrets" is the OLD, insecure way. │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

10.5 Security Contexts & Container Runtime Security

Security contexts control the runtime behavior of pods and containers. They're the last line of defense — even if an attacker compromises the application code, a properly configured security context limits the damage they can do:

📖 Pod-Level vs Container-Level Security Context

Security contexts can be set at TWO levels: Pod-level (spec.securityContext) — applies to ALL containers in the pod. Container-level (spec.containers[].securityContext) — overrides pod-level per container. Container-level settings take PRECEDENCE. Set defaults at pod level, override at container level when needed.

The Six Critical Security Context Fields

FieldPSA RestrictedWhat It DoesWhy It Matters
runAsNonRootMUST be trueContainer runs as UID ≠ 0 (non-root)If attacker compromises app, they don't get root on the node. Single most important setting.
readOnlyRootFilesystemMUST be trueRoot filesystem is mounted read-onlyAttacker can't install malware, modify binaries, or write to /usr. Use emptyDir for /tmp.
capabilities.dropMUST drop ALLRemove ALL Linux capabilitiesEven as root IN the container, no cap_sys_admin, cap_net_raw, etc. Severely limited kernel access.
seccompProfileMUST be setRestricts available syscallsRuntimeDefault blocks ~44 dangerous syscalls. Custom profiles can block even more. Seccomp = syscall firewall.
allowPrivilegeEscalationMUST be falsePrevents setuid binaries from escalatingEven if a binary has the setuid bit, the kernel will NOT elevate privileges. Defense against container escapes.
runAsUser / runAsGroupRecommendedExplicit UID/GID for the containerDeterministic — you know EXACTLY what UID the process runs as. Without this, it uses the image's default USER.

anihpj Security Context — The Canonical Spec

anihpj-security-context.yaml — Production-Ready Pod Security 
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: anihpj-api
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  # ─── POD-LEVEL: Defaults for ALL containers ───
  securityContext:
    runAsNonRoot: true
    runAsUser: 1000
    runAsGroup: 3000
    fsGroup: 3000          # Filesystem group for volume mounts

  containers:
  - name: api
    image: registry.anihpj.com/jobpost:v2.1
    # ─── CONTAINER-LEVEL ───
    securityContext:
      runAsNonRoot: true
      readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
      allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
      capabilities:
        drop:
        - ALL              # Drop EVERYTHING
      seccompProfile:
        type: RuntimeDefault
    volumeMounts:
    - name: tmp
      mountPath: /tmp      # /tmp needs writes → emptyDir
    - name: cache
      mountPath: /var/cache
  volumes:
  - name: tmp
    emptyDir: {}
  - name: cache
    emptyDir: {}

# ✅ PSA RESTRICTED CHECK: ALL required fields present.
#    kubectl apply -f anihpj-api.yaml → SUCCESS (no admission denial)

Linux Capabilities — Why "drop: [ALL]" Is the Single Most Important Setting

Linux capabilities break the monolithic "root" privilege into 40+ granular permissions. A process with full capabilities can do ANYTHING — load kernel modules, change network config, read any file, kill any process. Dropping ALL capabilities is the SINGLE most effective security measure you can apply to a container. Here's what you're actually preventing:

CapabilityWhat Root Could Do With ItContainer Impact If Dropped
CAP_SYS_ADMINMount filesystems, change namespaces, load kernel modules, access /dev/mem. The "new root" — most powerful capability. Exploited in MOST container escape CVEs.Cannot mount filesystems. Cannot change namespaces (prevents container escape). Cannot load kernel modules. This is THE critical capability to drop.
CAP_NET_RAWCreate raw sockets. Send arbitrary packets. ICMP ping. ARP spoofing. SYN scanning. DNS poisoning.Cannot craft raw packets. ping still works (uses ICMP sockets, not raw). But attacker can't ARP-spoof, SYN-scan, or craft malicious DNS responses.
CAP_SYS_PTRACETrace any process on the system. Read /proc/<pid>/mem. Inject code into running processes. Dump credentials from other containers' memory.Cannot trace other processes. Attacker inside compromised container can't dump memory of other containers or inject code into them.
CAP_SYS_BOOTReboot the system. kexec into a new kernel.Cannot reboot the node. Compromised container can't take down the entire node.
CAP_SYS_MODULELoad and unload kernel modules. Insert rootkits directly into the kernel.Cannot load kernel modules. Blocks kernel-level rootkits. Combined with seccomp, makes kernel-level attacks extremely difficult.
CAP_SYS_TIMEChange the system clock. Disrupt TLS certificate validation (time-based). Disrupt log timestamps.Cannot change system time. TLS cert validation remains intact. Log timestamps remain trustworthy.

How Capabilities, Seccomp, and AppArmor Work Together

These three security mechanisms operate at different levels. Defense-in-depth means using ALL three — capabilities restrict WHAT privileged operations are available, seccomp restricts WHICH syscalls can be called, and AppArmor/SELinux restrict WHICH files and resources can be accessed:

DEFENSE-IN-DEPTH — Capabilities + Seccomp + AppArmor/SELinux
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                 │
  │  USER SPACE                                                      │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │  DOCKER CONTAINER (anihpj-api)                             │ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │  Application: python manage.py runserver                  │ │
  │  │       │                                                    │ │
  │  │       │ Makes a syscall: open("/etc/shadow", O_RDONLY)    │ │
  │  │       ▼                                                    │ │
  │  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ │
  │  │  │ LAYER 3: AppArmor / SELinux (MANDATORY ACCESS CONTROL)│ │ │
  │  │  │ "Your profile says you can ONLY read /app/** and     │ │ │
  │  │  │  /tmp/**. /etc/shadow is NOT in the allowlist.       │ │ │
  │  │  │  → ACCESS DENIED (-EACCES)"                          │ │ │
  │  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │ │
  │  │       │ (if AppArmor allowed it, would continue...)      │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                 │
  │  KERNEL SPACE                                                    │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │       │ (syscall reaches the kernel)                       │ │
  │  │       ▼                                                    │ │
  │  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ │
  │  │  │ LAYER 2: SECCOMP (SYSCALL FILTERING)                │ │ │
  │  │  │ "RuntimeDefault profile says open() and read() are  │ │ │
  │  │  │  allowed, but mount(), reboot(), and kexec() are    │ │ │
  │  │  │  NOT. → 44 of 300+ syscalls BLOCKED."              │ │ │
  │  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │ │
  │  │       │ (if seccomp allowed it, would continue...)       │ │
  │  │       ▼                                                    │ │
  │  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ │
  │  │  │ LAYER 1: CAPABILITIES (PRIVILEGE CHECKING)          │ │ │
  │  │  │ "This syscall requires CAP_SYS_ADMIN. Your container│ │ │
  │  │  │  dropped ALL capabilities → you don't have it.      │ │ │
  │  │  │  → OPERATION NOT PERMITTED (-EPERM)"               │ │ │
  │  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                 │
  │  💡 THE STACK: AppArmor blocks at the FILE level. Seccomp       │
  │     blocks at the SYSCALL level. Capabilities block at the      │
  │     PRIVILEGE level. All three must fail for an attacker to     │
  │     succeed. Remove any one layer, and the attacker has a path. │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

10.6 Secrets Encryption at Rest

By default, Kubernetes Secrets stored in etcd are base64-ENCODED, NOT encrypted. Base64 is an encoding — anyone with etcd access can decode it instantly. This is the #1 Kubernetes security misconception that the CNPA exam WILL test:

SECRETS ENCRYPTION — Before vs After
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                 │
  │  ❌ WITHOUT ENCRYPTION (Default — DANGEROUS):                    │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │  Secret YAML:                    etcd stores:              │ │
  │  │  data:                           /registry/secrets/       │ │
  │  │    DB_PASSWORD: c2VjdXJlcHc=    ─▶  DB_PASSWORD:          │ │
  │  │                                  │    c2VjdXJlcHc=         │ │
  │  │  (base64 of "securepw")          │                         │ │
  │  │                                  │  ANYONE with etcd       │ │
  │  │                                  │  access can:            │ │
  │  │                                  │  $ echo "c2VjdXJlcHc=" │ │
  │  │                                  │    | base64 -d          │ │
  │  │                                  │  → "securepw" 🔓        │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                 │
  │  ✅ WITH ENCRYPTION (EncryptionConfiguration):                   │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │  Secret YAML:                                            │ │
  │  │  data:                                                   │ │
  │  │    DB_PASSWORD: c2VjdXJlcHc=                             │ │
  │  │       │                                                   │ │
  │  │       ▼ K8s API Server intercepts WRITE                   │ │
  │  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │ │
  │  │  │  EncryptionConfiguration:                         │    │ │
  │  │  │  - resources: [secrets]                           │    │ │
  │  │  │    providers:                                     │    │ │
  │  │  │    - aescbc:                                      │    │ │
  │  │  │        keys:                                      │    │ │
  │  │  │        - name: key1                               │    │ │
  │  │  │          secret: <base64-encoded-32-byte-key>     │    │ │
  │  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │ │
  │  │       │                                                   │ │
  │  │       ▼ API Server encrypts with AES-CBC-256              │ │
  │  │  etcd stores:                                             │ │
  │  │    DB_PASSWORD: k8s:enc:aescbc:v1:key1:<ciphertext>      │ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │  Attacker with etcd access sees: CIPHERTEXT (useless!) 🔒 │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                 │
  │  💡 BASE64 IS ENCODING, NOT ENCRYPTION.                         │
  │     Encoding = reversible without a key (like ASCII).           │
  │     Encryption = reversible ONLY with the correct key.          │
  │     This distinction is ALWAYS tested on the CNPA exam.         │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Enabling Encryption — Step by Step

EncryptionConfiguration — Enable Secrets Encryption 
# 1. Generate a 32-byte encryption key:
#    head -c 32 /dev/urandom | base64

# 2. Create EncryptionConfiguration:
apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1
kind: EncryptionConfiguration
resources:
- resources:
  - secrets                    # Encrypt Secrets
  - configmaps                 # Optionally encrypt ConfigMaps too
  providers:
  - aescbc:                    # AES-CBC 256-bit encryption
      keys:
      - name: key1
        secret: Yjg0ZzRqOH...  # Your 32-byte base64 key
  - identity: {}               # Fallback: plain text (for migration)

# 3. Configure kube-apiserver to use it:
#    In /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml:
#    --encryption-provider-config=/etc/kubernetes/encryption-config.yaml

# 4. Mount the config file into the API server pod:
#    volumeMounts:
#    - name: encryption-config
#      mountPath: /etc/kubernetes/encryption-config.yaml
#      readOnly: true
#    volumes:
#    - name: encryption-config
#      hostPath:
#        path: /etc/kubernetes/encryption-config.yaml
#        type: File

# 5. VERIFY encryption is active:
#    kubectl get secret anihpj-db-creds -o json | jq '.metadata.annotations'
#    # Look for: "encryption.kubernetes.io/encrypted": "true"

# 6. RE-ENCRYPT all existing secrets:
#    kubectl get secrets -A -o json | kubectl replace -f -
#    # This forces re-write through the encryption provider
⚠️ Encryption Key Management — Critical for CNPA

The encryption key is stored in a FILE on the control plane node. If an attacker gets root on the control plane, they can read the key AND etcd — encryption is defeated. Mitigations: (1) Use a KMS plugin (AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, GCP Cloud KMS) instead of local keys for production. (2) Rotate keys regularly — EncryptionConfiguration supports multiple keys for smooth rotation. (3) Restrict control plane access — only platform admins should have SSH/API access.

⚠️ Encryption Key Management — Critical for CNPA

The encryption key is stored in a FILE on the control plane node. If an attacker gets root on the control plane, they can read the key AND etcd — encryption is defeated. Mitigations: (1) Use a KMS plugin (AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, GCP Cloud KMS) instead of local keys for production. (2) Rotate keys regularly — EncryptionConfiguration supports multiple keys for smooth rotation. (3) Restrict control plane access — only platform admins should have SSH/API access.

KMS Plugin — Production-Grade Key Management

For production, use a KMS plugin instead of storing the encryption key locally. The KMS plugin encrypts the local AES key WITH a cloud KMS key — adding an additional layer of protection:

KMS Encryption Configuration — AWS KMS Example 
apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1
kind: EncryptionConfiguration
resources:
- resources:
  - secrets
  providers:
  - kms:                          # KMS PLUGIN (production)
      apiVersion: v2
      name: aws-kms-provider
      endpoint: unix:///var/run/kmsplugin/socket.sock
      cachesize: 1000             # Cache decrypted DEKs
      timeout: 3s
  - aescbc:                        # LOCAL KEY (fallback for migration)
      keys:
      - name: key1
        secret: <base64-key>
  - identity: {}                   # Plain text (last resort)

# HOW KMS PLUGIN WORKS:
# 1. API server generates a Data Encryption Key (DEK) locally
# 2. DEK is sent to the KMS plugin
# 3. KMS plugin encrypts DEK with cloud KMS → encrypted DEK stored in etcd
# 4. To decrypt: encrypted DEK → KMS plugin → cloud KMS decrypts → DEK → decrypt secret
#
# 💡 ADVANTAGE OVER LOCAL KEYS:
# Even if attacker steals etcd data + encryption config file,
# they CANNOT decrypt without access to the cloud KMS key.
# Cloud KMS has its own IAM permissions, audit logging, and key rotation.

10.7 Practice Lab — 10 CNPA Exam-Style Questions

Test your understanding of the 4 C's, AAA, RBAC, ServiceAccounts, Security Contexts, and Secrets Encryption.

Security Q1 of 10
Which of the 4 C's does RBAC belong to?
A) Code — RBAC is configured in YAML files which are code
B) Container — RBAC controls which containers can run
C) Cloud — RBAC is managed by cloud IAM
D) Cluster — RBAC controls access to the Kubernetes API and resources within the cluster
✅ Correct Answer: D — RBAC is a Cluster-layer security control

The 4 C's map as: Code (SAST, dependency scanning, secrets detection), Container (image scanning, signing, non-root user), Cluster (RBAC, PSA, NetworkPolicies, etcd encryption), Cloud (IAM, VPC, KMS). RBAC is purely a K8s cluster mechanism — it controls who can access the K8s API and what they can do with cluster resources.

Security Q2 of 10
A user runs kubectl and gets "Error from server (Forbidden): deployments.apps is forbidden." Which AAA gate failed?
A) Authorization (AuthZ) — the user is authenticated but RBAC doesn't allow this action
B) Authentication (AuthN) — the user's certificate is invalid
C) Admission Control — a Kyverno policy blocked the request
D) etcd — the API server couldn't write to the database
✅ Correct Answer: A — "Forbidden" = AuthZ (RBAC) failure

The AAA error messages are distinct: "401 Unauthorized" → AuthN (bad cert/token). "403 Forbidden" or "forbidden" → AuthZ (RBAC doesn't permit the action). "admission webhook denied" → Admission (policy blocked it). This is a CRITICAL debugging skill for the CNPA exam — identify the failing gate from the error message alone.

Security Q3 of 10
The anihpj-developers group needs to manage Deployments in the anihpj-dev namespace. Which RBAC objects do you need?
A) ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding — Deployments are cluster-scoped
B) Role (namespace: anihpj-dev) + RoleBinding (namespace: anihpj-dev) — Deployments are namespace-scoped
C) ClusterRole + RoleBinding — ClusterRoles can be bound in a specific namespace
D) Just a Role — no binding needed for groups
✅ Correct Answer: B — Role + RoleBinding in the same namespace

Deployments are namespace-scoped resources (they live in a specific namespace). A Role (namespace-scoped) is sufficient. A RoleBinding binds it to the group within the SAME namespace. C is technically valid (you CAN use ClusterRole + RoleBinding to reuse permissions across namespaces), but B is the most specific and least-privilege answer — which is always the CNPA-preferred choice.

Security Q4 of 10
You need a ServiceAccount for the anihpj-api pod that ONLY needs to read one specific Secret. What's the correct approach?
A) Use the default ServiceAccount in the namespace — it already has necessary permissions
B) Create a ClusterRole with secrets read access and bind it cluster-wide
C) Create a dedicated SA + Role scoped to the SINGLE secret by resourceName + RoleBinding in the pod's namespace
D) Mount the secret as an environment variable — no ServiceAccount needed
✅ Correct Answer: C — Dedicated SA + Role scoped to one Secret by name

Least privilege: create a Role that grants get on secrets with resourceNames: [db-credentials] ONLY in the pod's namespace. Create a dedicated SA, bind the Role to it, and set serviceAccountName on the pod. A) Default SA is too permissive. B) ClusterRole + cluster-wide binding violates least privilege. D) Env vars expose secrets to anyone who can kubectl describe pod or access the pod's /proc.

Security Q5 of 10
Which security context combination satisfies PSA Restricted requirements?
A) runAsNonRoot: false, capabilities.drop: [ALL] — root is OK if all capabilities are dropped
B) runAsNonRoot: true, readOnlyRootFilesystem: false — as long as non-root, writable FS is fine
C) runAsNonRoot: true, seccompProfile: Unconfined — seccomp is optional under Restricted
D) runAsNonRoot: true, readOnlyRootFilesystem: true, capabilities.drop: [ALL], allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, seccompProfile: RuntimeDefault
✅ Correct Answer: D — All 5 fields must be set correctly

PSA Restricted requires ALL of: runAsNonRoot: true (A fails — root is never OK under Restricted), readOnlyRootFilesystem: true (B fails), capabilities.drop: [ALL] (must drop ALL, not just some), allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, seccompProfile set to RuntimeDefault or Localhost (C fails — Unconfined is not allowed). Missing ANY one of these → PSA Restricted admission denial.

Security Q6 of 10
What's the difference between base64 encoding and encryption of Kubernetes Secrets?
A) Base64 is REVERSIBLE without a key — anyone can decode it. Encryption requires a cryptographic key to decrypt. Default K8s Secrets use base64 ONLY — NOT encryption.
B) Base64 IS encryption — that's why it's called "base64 encryption"
C) Secrets are encrypted by default in etcd — no additional configuration needed
D) Base64 and encryption are the same thing with different names
✅ Correct Answer: A — Base64 = encoding (no key needed), Encryption = needs a key

Base64 is a CHARACTER ENCODING — it converts binary data to ASCII text. It's trivially reversible: echo "c2VjdXJlcHc=" | base64 -d → "securepw". No key required. Default K8s Secrets are stored as base64-encoded values in etcd — ANYONE with etcd access can read them in plaintext. Encryption (via EncryptionConfiguration with AES-CBC) requires a cryptographic key to decrypt. This is the most important K8s security distinction — tested on EVERY CNPA exam.

Security Q7 of 10
An attacker gains access to a pod's ServiceAccount token. What limits the damage?
A) Nothing — ServiceAccount tokens have cluster-admin by default
B) RBAC (the SA's Role limits what it can do) + Token expiry (short-lived tokens auto-expire) + Token binding (token is bound to the specific pod)
C) NetworkPolicies — they prevent the token from being used outside the pod
D) The token is encrypted, so the attacker can't read it
✅ Correct Answer: B — RBAC + token expiry + pod binding = defense-in-depth

Three layers limit the blast radius: (1) RBAC: If the SA only has a Role scoped to read one Secret, the attacker can ONLY read that one Secret — not list pods, not delete anything. (2) Token expiry: K8s 1.22+ projected tokens expire in 1 hour. Even if stolen, the window of abuse is limited. (3) Token binding: The token is bound to the specific pod's UID — it can't be reused from a different pod. A) False — default SA has limited permissions unless explicitly granted. C) NetworkPolicies control pod-to-pod traffic, not token usage. D) Tokens are not encrypted at rest within the pod filesystem.

Security Q8 of 10
Which command helps you debug why a user can't create Deployments?
A) kubectl get secrets — it shows authentication tokens
B) kubectl describe pod — it shows the pod's security context
C) kubectl auth can-i create deployments --as alice -n anihpj-dev — it checks RBAC permissions for a specific user/action/namespace
D) kubectl logs kube-apiserver — it shows admission webhook decisions
✅ Correct Answer: C — kubectl auth can-i is the RBAC debugging tool

kubectl auth can-i <verb> <resource> --as <user> -n <namespace> is the ESSENTIAL RBAC debugging command. It simulates an API request as a specific user and checks whether RBAC would allow it. Returns yes or no. Add --list to see ALL permissions for a user. This is the first command you should run when anyone says "I can't do X" — it instantly tells you if RBAC is the problem.

Security Q9 of 10
You discover a pod running as root (UID 0) with writable root filesystem in the anihpj-prod namespace. What's the most likely root cause?
A) The pod's securityContext is missing runAsNonRoot: true and readOnlyRootFilesystem: true — and PSA Restricted is not enforced on the namespace
B) Someone SSH'd into the node and changed the container's UID manually
C) The container image was built with a root USER instruction — this overrides all Kubernetes settings
D) Kyverno is misconfigured — it should have automatically changed the UID
✅ Correct Answer: A — Missing securityContext + PSA not enforced

Two failures occurred: (1) The pod spec omitted runAsNonRoot: true and readOnlyRootFilesystem: true in its securityContext, allowing it to run as root with writable FS. (2) PSA Restricted is NOT enforced on the anihpj-prod namespace — if it were, the pod would have been REJECTED at creation time. C is incorrect — even if the image's USER is root, Kubernetes runAsNonRoot: true OVERRIDES the image's USER. B is unlikely and not the root cause. D is wrong — Kyverno Mutate CAN add security contexts, but it's not automatic unless a mutate policy exists. The remediation: add the securityContext AND enforce PSA Restricted on the namespace.

Security Q10 of 10
Which approach provides the STRONGEST security for anihpj's platform?
A) Enable just PSA Restricted — it covers all security requirements
B) All 4 C's layered: SAST in CI (Code) + Trivy scan + Cosign sign (Container) + RBAC + PSA + NetworkPolicy + Secrets Encryption (Cluster) + IAM + VPC + KMS (Cloud)
C) A strong password on the kubeconfig — authentication is the most important layer
D) Run everything as root in privileged mode — it simplifies operations
✅ Correct Answer: B — All 4 C's layered = defense-in-depth

The 4 C's principle: an attacker must breach ALL four layers. PSA Restricted (Cluster layer) is strong but doesn't protect against vulnerable code (Code layer) or compromised base images (Container layer). IAM and VPC (Cloud layer) don't protect against insider threats with cluster access. Only layering ALL four — SAST in CI, image scanning and signing, cluster RBAC+PSA+NetworkPolicy+encryption, and cloud IAM+KMS — provides defense-in-depth. If ANY layer fails, the others still protect the platform. D is the OPPOSITE of security. C is just one gate (AuthN). A covers only pod security contexts.

📊 Chapter 10 Summary — Key Takeaways

🎯4 C'sCode→Container→Cluster→Cloud. Attacker must breach ALL four. Every layer is essential.
🚦AAA FlowAuthN (401)→AuthZ (403)→Admission (webhook denied). Error message tells you which gate failed.
🔑RBACRole/ClusterRole = permissions. RoleBinding/ClusterRoleBinding = who gets them. Least privilege always.
🤖ServiceAccountsPod identity. Never use default SA. Dedicated SA + scoped Role + short-lived projected tokens.
🛡️Security ContextrunAsNonRoot, readOnlyRootFS, drop ALL caps, seccomp RuntimeDefault. Non-negotiable for Restricted.
🔐Secrets EncryptionBase64 ≠ encryption. EncryptionConfiguration with AES-256. KMS plugin for production key management.

Chapter 11: Security in CI/CD Pipelines — Shift-Left & Supply Chain Integrity

Security can't wait until deployment. By the time an image reaches the cluster, it's too late — vulnerabilities are baked in, unsigned images are indistinguishable from legitimate ones, and leaked credentials have already been used. Shift-left security means integrating security checks at EVERY stage of the CI/CD pipeline — from pre-commit hooks to runtime detection. This chapter covers the complete security toolchain: SAST, secret detection, vulnerability scanning, image signing, SBOM generation, OIDC authentication, and the SLSA framework — all applied to the anihpj/jobpost pipeline.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~2 hours 🔒 CI/CD Security 🎯 Domain 2: 20% 📦 Supply Chain

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Shift-Left Security — integrating security checks at pre-commit, PR, build, deploy, and runtime stages
  • ✅ Image Vulnerability Scanning — Trivy/Grype for CVE detection. Severity-based pipeline gates (CRITICAL→fail, HIGH→block)
  • ✅ Image Signing & Verification — Cosign + Sigstore keyless signing. Kyverno VerifyImages to enforce only signed images run
  • ✅ SBOM (Software Bill of Materials) — Syft to generate CycloneDX/SPDX. "Nutrition label" for container images
  • ✅ Pipeline Security — OIDC for temporary credentials (no static keys!). SLSA Framework levels 1-4 for supply chain integrity
