15.1 What is GitOps? — Git is the Source of Truth

GitOps is an operating model for cloud native applications that uses Git repositories as the single source of truth for declarative infrastructure and application configuration. An automated process ensures that the running cluster state matches the desired state defined in Git. If there's a drift — the agent corrects it automatically. If you need to change the application — you change Git, not the cluster:

🔍 The Problem GitOps Solves — Before and After

To truly understand WHY GitOps exists, you need to see the operational nightmare it replaces. Before GitOps, platform teams lived in a world of manual kubectl commands, snowflake clusters, and deployment anxiety. GitOps doesn't just automate — it fundamentally changes the relationship between developers, operators, and the cluster:

ProblemBefore GitOpsAfter GitOps
"What's running in production?"Nobody knows exactly. Someone ran kubectl apply 3 weeks ago. Another person scaled replicas manually during an incident. The cluster is a snowflake — unique and irreproducible.Git IS the answer. git log shows every change. ArgoCD ensures the cluster matches Git. The cluster is cattle — disposable and reproducible.
"Who changed the replicas from 3 to 10?"Slack archaeology. "I think Alice did it during the outage?" No audit trail. No accountability. Changes happen directly on the cluster with no record.git log -- apps/anihpj/overlays/prod/ shows the commit, author, timestamp, PR number, and reviewer. Complete audit trail in one command.
"How do we recover from a disaster?"Hope the Terraform state is current. Hope someone documented the manual steps. Rebuild from memory. Recovery takes hours or days. Some things are permanently lost.Point ArgoCD at a new cluster. All 45+ applications auto-sync within minutes. Recovery = redeploy from Git. No state lost. No tribal knowledge needed.
"Is staging the same as production?"Probably not. Someone patched production directly. Staging has different resource limits. "It worked in staging!" is a meaningless statement because environments have diverged.Same Git repo, same manifests, different Kustomize overlays. The ONLY difference is the overlay values (replicas, resources). What you test in staging IS what runs in production.
"How do we deploy?"Run the CI pipeline. Hope the KUBECONFIG secret is still valid. Hope nobody changed the cluster between the last deploy and now. Deployment is an event — with anxiety attached.Merge a PR. ArgoCD detects the change. Syncs automatically. Deployment is a state — the cluster continuously converges to Git. No ceremony. No credentials outside the cluster.
💡 The Mental Model Shift

Traditional ops thinks: "I TELL the cluster what to do" (imperative). GitOps thinks: "I DECLARE what the cluster SHOULD BE, and an agent makes it so" (declarative, reconciled). This shift from pushing commands to declaring state is the fundamental insight behind GitOps. Once you internalize this, every GitOps concept — pull model, self-heal, pruning, drift detection — becomes obvious.

AspectTraditional CI/CD (Push)GitOps (Pull)

💡 CNPA Exam Insight

GitOps is not a TOOL — it's an OPERATING MODEL. ArgoCD and Flux are implementations. The exam tests your understanding of the MODEL: Git as SSOT, pull-based reconciliation, and continuous drift correction. You should also know that GitOps is a CNCF Incubating project originally created by Weaveworks.

📈 The GitOps Maturity Ladder — Where Is Your Organization?

Not all "GitOps" is equal. Organizations evolve through stages of maturity. The CNPA exam focuses on Level 3+ — the pull-based, reconciled model. Knowing the levels helps you identify what IS and ISN'T GitOps on the exam:

LvlNameHow It WorksGitOps?Example
0No GitOpskubectl apply from local laptop. No history. No audit.❌kubectl apply -f . from dev machine
1Git + ManualYAML stored in Git repo. Human manually runs kubectl apply after pull.⚠️ Partialgit pull && kubectl apply -f ./manifests

📖 CNPA Tip

The exam will present scenarios and ask "Is this GitOps?" — the answer is YES only if the agent PULLS from Git and runs INSIDE the cluster (Level 3+). "I put my YAML in Git and my CI deploys it" is Level 2 — NOT GitOps by CNPA standards. Remember: Pull + In-Cluster Agent = GitOps. Push from CI = Not GitOps.

🧭 What GitOps IS and ISN'T — Clearing the Confusion

✅
GitOps IS...

• An operating model, not a tool
• Git as the single source of truth for desired state
• Pull-based: agents inside the cluster pull from Git
• Continuously reconciled: drift is auto-corrected
• Declarative: desired state, not imperative commands
• Versioned: every change is a Git commit
• Self-healing: manual edits are auto-reverted

❌
GitOps is NOT...

• Just "putting YAML in Git" — that's config management
• ArgoCD or Flux specifically — those are implementations
• A CI pipeline that runs kubectl apply (that's push CD)
• GitHub Actions with a KUBECONFIG secret
• Manual git pull → kubectl apply workflows
• Terraform Cloud or infrastructure-as-code alone
• Only for Kubernetes (principles apply broadly)

15.2 The 4 GitOps Principles — Weaveworks' Foundation

Weaveworks (the creator of GitOps and Flux) defined four principles that every GitOps system must follow. These aren't optional — they're what separates GitOps from "I put my YAML in Git and run kubectl apply." The CNPA exam expects you to know and recognize these four:

📋
1. Declarative

The entire system must be described declaratively — not imperatively. You declare "I want 3 replicas" — not "run kubectl scale." K8s YAML, Helm charts, and Kustomize overlays are all declarative. Why: Declarative config can be versioned, reviewed, and diffed. Imperative commands cannot.

📦
2. Versioned & Immutable

The desired state is versioned in Git and immutable. Every change is a commit with author, timestamp, and message. Why: Complete audit trail. Know WHO changed WHAT and WHEN. Rollback = git revert. No guessing what version is running.

⬇️
3. Pulled Automatically

Software agents automatically pull the desired state from Git and apply it. No manual kubectl. No CI push. Agents run INSIDE the cluster. Why: No external credentials. Cluster pulls — not pushes. More secure. Agents auto-detect new commits.

🔄
4. Continuously Reconciled

Agents continuously monitor actual state vs desired state and reconcile drift. If someone manually edits a Deployment, the agent reverts it. Why: Keeps the cluster in sync. Prevents configuration drift. Self-healing. Self-correcting.

🧩 Declarative vs Imperative — Why Principle 1 Matters Most

The first principle (Declarative) is the foundation for all the others. If your config isn't declarative, it can't be versioned, pulled, or reconciled. Here's the practical difference — using anihpj's jobpost deployment:

✅ DECLARATIVE (GitOps Way)

You write WHAT you want:

# deployment.yaml — desired state in Git
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: jobpost
spec:
  replicas: 3
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: jobpost
        image: anihpj/jobpost:v2.4.1

Agent does the work: ArgoCD reads this file, compares to cluster, and ensures 3 replicas of v2.4.1 are running. You never run kubectl commands.

Why it works for GitOps: This file can be versioned in Git (Principle 2), pulled by ArgoCD (Principle 3), and continuously reconciled (Principle 4).

❌ IMPERATIVE (NOT GitOps)

You tell HOW to do it:

# Terminal commands — no record, no audit
$ kubectl scale deployment jobpost --replicas=3
$ kubectl set image deployment/jobpost \
  jobpost=anihpj/jobpost:v2.4.1
$ kubectl rollout status deployment/jobpost

You do the work: Every command must be remembered, executed in order, and manually verified. If you forget a step, the cluster is in an unknown state.

Why it FAILS for GitOps: No version history (violates P2), nothing to pull (violates P3), no reconciliation possible (violates P4). The cluster state is whatever the last kubectl command left it as.

📖 The Litmus Test

To determine if something is declarative, ask: "Can I store this in Git, and can a machine read it and make the world match it?" If yes (YAML, JSON, HCL) → declarative. If no (shell scripts, kubectl commands, click-ops) → imperative. GitOps ONLY works with declarative configuration. This is the single most important concept the CNPA exam tests about Principle 1.

🧠 THE 4 PRINCIPLES AS A SYSTEM
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  PRINCIPLE           HOW IT'S MET            VIOLATION                │
│                                                                       │
│  1. DECLARATIVE      YAML in Git             kubectl scale --replicas │
│                       "replicas: 3"           (imperative, not in Git) │
│                                                                       │

│                       git log = audit         No who/when/why         │
│                                                                       │

│                                                                       │

│                                                                       │

⚠️ What Happens When a Principle is Violated?

Each GitOps principle exists for a reason. Violating any one of them degrades the system. The CNPA exam tests your ability to identify WHICH principle is broken in a given scenario:

Principle ViolatedScenarioConsequenceFix
1. DeclarativeOps team runs kubectl set image to patch productionCluster state unknown. No record of the change. Can't reproduce.Define the image tag in deployment.yaml in Git. Let ArgoCD sync it.
2. VersionedSomeone directly edits YAML on the server with no commitNo audit trail. Can't answer "who changed replicas from 3 to 10?"All changes through Git PRs with mandatory reviews.
3. Pulled AutoCI pipeline (GitHub Actions) stores KUBECONFIG and runs kubectl applyCI compromise = cluster compromise. External attack vector.Move ArgoCD inside cluster. Remove KUBECONFIG from CI.
4. ReconciledSelf-heal disabled. Engineer runs kubectl edit deploy and forgetsDrift accumulates over months. "Snowflake" cluster. DR impossible.Enable self-heal. All manual changes must go through Git.

💡 Memory Aid: The 4 Principles Mnemonic

D-V-P-R = Declarative, Versioned, Pulled, Reconciled. Think: "Don't Violate Pull Requests" — because in GitOps, every change goes through a PR (pull request), and the agent pulls from Git. If you see ALL FOUR in a scenario description, it's GitOps. If any one is missing, it's NOT full GitOps.

15.3 Push vs Pull Deployment Models — Why GitOps Prefers PULL

The fundamental architectural choice in deployment automation is: does an external system PUSH changes to the cluster, or does an internal agent PULL them from Git? GitOps firmly chooses PULL — and understanding WHY is essential for the CNPA exam:

✅ PULL MODEL (GitOps — ArgoCD / Flux)

How it works: Agent runs INSIDE the cluster. Watches Git repo for changes. Pulls manifests and applies them. Continuously reconciles.

Security: Credentials stored ONLY in cluster. No external system has cluster admin access. Attack surface minimal.

Disaster Recovery: Point ArgoCD at a new cluster → all 45 apps synced automatically. Minutes.

Drift Detection: Self-heal. Manual kubectl edit → auto-reverted within 3 minutes.

anihpj: ArgoCD watches github.com/anihpj/gitops → syncs to staging → syncs to prod.

⚠️ PUSH MODEL (Traditional CI/CD)

How it works: CI system (GitHub Actions, Jenkins) runs kubectl apply against the cluster from outside.

Security: CI system stores kubeconfig. CI compromise = full cluster access. Broader attack surface.

Disaster Recovery: Re-run 45 CI pipelines. Hours. Dependency ordering matters.

Drift Detection: None. Manual kubectl edit stays until next pipeline run.

anihpj (old): GitHub Actions ran kubectl apply after build. Required KUBECONFIG secret in CI.

⚠️ Security: The #1 Reason GitOps is PULL

In Push: Your CI system stores cluster credentials (kubeconfig). If CI is compromised, your cluster is compromised. In Pull: Credentials stay INSIDE the cluster. ArgoCD/Flux has the kubeconfig — no external system does. The agent only reads from Git (which is public or has read-only deploy keys). This is the CNPA's preferred security posture.

│                       │     CLUSTER          │                       │
│                       │  ⚠️ Crypto miner     │  ← Still bad!          │
│                       │  deployed!            │    But:               │
│                       └──────────────────────┘                       │
│                                                                       │
│  THE KEY DIFFERENCE:                                                  │
│  • Push: Attacker has DIRECT cluster access. Full control.            │
│  • Pull: Attacker must go through Git (auditable, requires PR review  │
│    in a proper setup). ArgoCD only applies what's in Git.             │
│                                                                       │
│  DEFENSE IN DEPTH for Pull:                                           │
│  1. Git branch protection (require PR reviews)                        │
│  2. ArgoCD RBAC (who can create/modify Applications)                  │
│  3. NetworkPolicy (ArgoCD can only talk to Git + target clusters)     │
│  4. Audit logs (who synced what, when)                                │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

🔄 Migration Path — Moving from Push to Pull (anihpj's Journey)

StepActionRisk LevelRollback
1Install ArgoCD in cluster (alongside existing push pipeline)🟢 LowDelete ArgoCD — push still works
2Create GitOps repo with app manifests (Kustomize/Helm)🟢 LowRepo is independent — no impact
3Create ArgoCD Application (manual sync ONLY — no auto-sync)🟡 MediumDelete Application. Push still live.
4Run push + ArgoCD in parallel for 1-2 weeks. Compare states.🟡 MediumPush is still the source of truth
5Enable ArgoCD automated sync. Disable push pipeline's kubectl apply step.🟠 HighRe-enable push pipeline step
6Remove KUBECONFIG secret from CI. GitOps is now the ONLY path.🟢 Low (done)N/A — GitOps is the new normal
💡 CNPA Exam Tip

The exam may ask: "A team wants to adopt GitOps but has an existing push pipeline. What's the safest migration approach?" Answer: Run both in parallel (dual-write) for a transition period. ArgoCD with manual sync first, then automated. Never "big bang" switch — let the push pipeline be the safety net while you validate ArgoCD behavior.

15.4 ArgoCD Architecture — The Pull Engine

ArgoCD is the CNCF-graduated GitOps tool. It runs inside the cluster and consists of three core components that work together to achieve GitOps reconciliation. Understanding how these pieces fit together is critical for CNPA:

🏗️ ARGOCD ARCHITECTURE — Core Components
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    ARGOCD ARCHITECTURE                                │
│                                                                       │
│  ┌────────────┐     ┌────────────────┐     ┌───────────────────┐     │
│  │    GIT     │     │   ARGOCD       │     │    KUBERNETES     │     │
│  │   REPO     │     │                │     │     CLUSTER       │     │
│  │            │     │ ┌────────────┐ │     │                   │     │

│  │ • Kustomize│     │ │ CLI + UI   │ │     │                   │     │
│  │            │     │ └─────┬──────┘ │     └───────────────────┘     │
│  │            │     │       │        │                               │

│  │            │     │ │ SERVER     │ │     │    CLUSTERS       │     │

│  │            │     │       │        │                               │

│  │            │     │ │ APPLICATION│ │                               │
│  │            │     │ │ CONTROLLER │ │                               │
│  │            │     │ │            │ │                               │

ArgoCD vs Flux — Two CNCF GitOps Tools

FeatureArgoCDFlux (v2)
CNCF StatusGraduatedGraduated
Web UI✅ Rich dashboard⚠️ Minimal (flux ui)
CLIargocd CLIflux CLI

🔀 Component Interaction Sequence — What Happens on Every Sync

⏱️ ARGOCD SYNC SEQUENCE — Step by Step
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  TIME    COMPONENT          ACTION                                    │
│  ────    ─────────          ──────                                    │
│  T+0s    App Controller     "Application CR changed or 3-min timer"  │
│          (The Brain)        → Sends request to Repo Server           │
│                                                                       │
│  T+0.5s  Repo Server        git clone/pull (incremental fetch)       │
│          (The Cloner)       → Reads path: apps/anihpj/overlays/prod   │
│                             → Detects: Kustomize overlay              │
│                             → Runs: kustomize build → final YAML      │
│                             → Caches result in Redis (TTL: 24h)       │
│                                                                       │
│  T+2s    Repo Server        Returns rendered manifests to Controller  │
│          → Controller       (list of K8s objects: Deploy, Svc, etc.)  │
│                                                                       │
│  T+2.5s  App Controller     kubectl get (all resources in namespace) │
│          (The Differ)       → Builds ACTUAL state from cluster        │
│                                                                       │
│  T+3s    App Controller     Three-way diff:                           │
│          (The Differ)       • Previous Git state (cached)             │
│                             • Current Git state (from Repo Server)    │
│                             • Live cluster state (from kubectl)       │
│                                                                       │
│  T+3.5s  App Controller     IF Diff = empty → App = "Synced" ✅      │
│          (Decision)         IF Diff has changes → schedule sync       │
│                                                                       │
│  T+4s    App Controller     IF syncPolicy.automated:                  │
│          (The Syncer)       → kubectl apply (changed resources)       │
│                             → kubectl delete (pruned resources)       │
│                             → Wait for resources to be Healthy        │
│                                                                       │
│  T+10s   App Controller     Update Application status:                │
│                             sync.status = "Synced"                    │
│                             health.status = "Healthy"                 │
│                                                                       │
│  T+10s   API Server         UI/CLI shows green checkmark             │
│                             Notifications sent (if configured)        │
│                                                                       │
│  T+180s  App Controller     Timer fires again → repeat from T+0s      │
│                             (Continuous reconciliation cycle)         │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

🩺 ArgoCD Application Health Status — Cheat Sheet

Health StatusMeaningCommon CausesAction
🟢 HealthyAll resources running as expectedNormal operationNone — this is the goal
🟡 ProgressingResources being created/updatedDeploy in progress, pod startingWait. If stuck > 5 min, investigate.
🔴 DegradedSome resources unhealthyCrashLoopBackOff, ImagePullBackOffCheck pod logs. Rollback if needed.
⏸️ SuspendedApplication paused (e.g., canary paused)Argo Rollouts paused canaryPromote or abort the rollout
❓ MissingResource not found in clusterManual deletion, never createdSync to recreate. Check pruning.
⚠️ UnknownHealth cannot be determinedCustom resource, no health check Lua scriptAdd custom health check. Monitor manually.
📖 Sync Status vs Health Status

Sync Status = Does the cluster match Git? (Synced / OutOfSync / Unknown). Health Status = Are the resources running properly? (Healthy / Progressing / Degraded). An app can be "Synced" but "Degraded" — Git says 3 replicas, cluster HAS 3 replicas, but all 3 are crashing. The CNPA exam expects you to distinguish between these two independent statuses.

🔐 ArgoCD RBAC & Projects — Who Can Do What?

ArgoCD has a built-in RBAC system controlling who can view, sync, or modify applications. Combined with AppProjects, you can create secure multi-tenant GitOps where Team A cannot touch Team B's apps:

👤
RBAC (Users & Permissions)

Built-in roles: role:admin (full access), role:readonly (view only). Custom policies: CSV policy rules defining who can sync/get/override specific apps. SSO: Integrates with OIDC (Okta, Azure AD, GitHub). anihpj: Backend team can sync jobpost/redis. Frontend team can sync web UI. Platform team = admin.

📦
AppProject (Resource Boundaries)

sourceRepos: Which Git repos can this project use? destinations: Which clusters/namespaces can this project deploy to? clusterResourceWhitelist: Which cluster-scoped resources are allowed? namespaceResourceBlacklist: Which resources are forbidden? anihpj: Project "anihpj-backend" → only github.com/anihpj/gitops → only namespace anihpj-* → no cluster-scoped resources.

🔔 ArgoCD Notifications — Staying Informed

ArgoCD Notifications is a separate controller that monitors Application events and sends alerts via Slack, Teams, email, webhook, or any other supported service. It uses triggers (when to notify) and templates (what to say):

TriggerFires When...Example Message
on-sync-succeededApplication sync completes successfully"✅ jobpost-prod synced commit abc123. Healthy."
on-sync-failedApplication sync fails"❌ jobpost-prod sync FAILED. manifest parse error."
on-health-degradedApplication health becomes Degraded"🔴 jobpost-staging is Degraded. 2/5 pods CrashLoopBackOff."
on-deployedApplication is fully synced and healthy"🚀 jobpost-prod v2.4.1 deployed successfully."
on-sync-runningSync has started but not yet completed"⏳ jobpost-staging sync in progress..."
💡 CNPA Exam Insight

ArgoCD Notifications is the expected answer for "how do you get alerted when a GitOps sync fails?" It's not part of ArgoCD core — it's a separate controller installed alongside ArgoCD. The exam may ask: "A team wants Slack notifications when a production Application becomes Degraded. What should they configure?" → ArgoCD Notifications with on-health-degraded trigger + Slack template.

🖥️ ArgoCD CLI Essentials — Operational Commands

The argocd CLI is how operators interact with ArgoCD day-to-day. While the Web UI is great for visualization, the CLI is essential for scripting, automation, and incident response. Here are the commands you must know for the CNPA exam:

BASHargocd CLI — Essential Commands
# ── LOGIN ──
argocd login <ARGOCD_SERVER> --sso           # Login via SSO (Okta, Azure AD)
argocd login <ARGOCD_SERVER> --username admin --password <PWD>

# ── APPLICATION MANAGEMENT ──
argocd app list                                # List ALL applications
argocd app get anihpj-prod                     # Detailed view of ONE app
argocd app sync anihpj-prod                    # MANUAL sync (applies Git to cluster)
argocd app sync anihpj-prod --prune            # Sync AND delete removed resources
argocd app diff anihpj-prod                    # PREVIEW what will change (dry-run!)
argocd app history anihpj-prod                 # Deployment history (commit SHAs)
argocd app rollback anihpj-prod <REVISION>     # Rollback to specific deployment

# ── EMERGENCY OPERATIONS ──
argocd app pause anihpj-prod                   # PAUSE sync (emergency fix mode)
argocd app resume anihpj-prod                  # RESUME sync after fixing
argocd app terminate-op anihpj-prod            # FORCE STOP a stuck sync operation

# ── CLUSTER MANAGEMENT ──
argocd cluster add <CLUSTER_CONTEXT>           # Register an external K8s cluster
argocd cluster list                             # List all connected clusters
argocd cluster rm <CLUSTER_URL>                 # Remove a cluster

📊 Sync Waves & Resource Hooks — Controlling Deployment Order

By default, ArgoCD applies all resources in parallel. But real applications have dependencies: a CRD must exist before its Custom Resource, a ConfigMap before the Deployment that references it, a database migration Job before the new pod starts. Sync waves control the ORDER of resource application within a single sync:

WaveApplied WhenTypical ResourcesExample
-10 to -1Before the main sync (pre-sync)CRDs, Namespaces, Network PoliciesInstall cert-manager CRDs before creating Certificate resources
0Default — first wave of main syncConfigMaps, Secrets, PVCsCreate DB connection ConfigMap before referencing it
1-5Core application resourcesDeployments, Services, Ingressesjobpost Deployment + Service + Ingress (order matters less)
6-10After core resources are healthyHPA, PDB, monitoring ServiceMonitorsHPA scales the Deployment → needs Deployment first
11+Last — post-sync cleanupJobs, cleanup CronJobsDatabase migration Job runs AFTER new pods are healthy

🪝 Resource Hooks — Run Actions During Sync

Hooks let you run Kubernetes resources (Jobs, Pods) at specific points in the sync lifecycle. Unlike regular resources that ArgoCD manages continuously, hooks run ONCE and are then ignored. This is how you run database migrations, smoke tests, or cleanup tasks as part of a GitOps sync:

Hook TypeRuns WhenUse CaseDeletion Policy
PreSyncBEFORE sync applies any resourcesDatabase backup before deploy, pre-flight checksBeforeHookCreation (default)
SyncAFTER PreSync, along with main resourcesDatabase migration Job, schema updatesHookSucceeded (delete after success)
SkipArgoCD SKIPS this resource entirelyResources managed externally (e.g., Terraform)N/A — never applied
PostSyncAFTER all resources are applied AND healthySmoke tests, integration tests, notification JobsHookSucceeded
SyncFailAFTER a sync FAILSCleanup tasks, notification of failureHookSucceeded
📖 anihpj Sync Wave Example

jobpost application sync order: Wave -5: Namespace created. Wave 0: ConfigMap (DB connection string), Secret (DB password). Wave 1: Deployment, Service, Ingress. PreSync Hook: DB backup Job runs. Sync Hook: Django migration Job (python manage.py migrate). PostSync Hook: Smoke test Job (curl /api/health). If migration fails → sync fails → old pods continue serving. If smoke test fails → sync is marked Failed, on-call is paged.

15.5 ArgoCD Application CRD — Defining WHAT and WHERE

The Application CRD is the core resource that tells ArgoCD WHAT to deploy and WHERE. It has two essential parts: Source (the Git repo with manifests) and Destination (the cluster + namespace to deploy to). The sync policy controls whether ArgoCD automatically applies changes or waits for manual approval:

YAMLanihpj-jobpost-application.yaml
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: anihpj-jobpost-staging
  namespace: argocd
  finalizers:
    - resources-finalizer.argocd.argoproj.io
spec:
  # ── PROJECT ──
  project: anihpj

  # ── SOURCE: WHERE the manifests live ──
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/anihpj/gitops.git
    targetRevision: main
    path: apps/anihpj/overlays/staging
    # Can use: Helm, Kustomize, Ksonnet, Jsonnet, or plain YAML

  # ── DESTINATION: WHERE to deploy ──
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc  # in-cluster
    namespace: anihpj-staging

  # ── SYNC POLICY ──
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true       # Delete resources that are no longer in Git
      selfHeal: true    # Revert manual kubectl edits
      allowEmpty: false # Don't sync if Git path is empty
    syncOptions:
      - CreateNamespace=true
      - PruneLast=true  # Prune AFTER new resources are healthy
    retry:
      limit: 5
      backoff:
        duration: 5s
        factor: 2
        maxDuration: 3m
📍
Source Fields (Required)

repoURL: Git repository URL (HTTPS or SSH). targetRevision: Branch, tag, or commit SHA. path: Directory containing manifests. Helm: Can also point to a Helm chart repo with values files.

🎯
Destination Fields (Required)

server: Cluster API server URL. Use https://kubernetes.default.svc for in-cluster. namespace: Target namespace. Must exist or CreateNamespace=true. Multiple destinations via ApplicationSet.

⚙️
Sync Policy (Optional but Recommended)

automated: Enables auto-sync. Without it, ArgoCD only detects OutOfSync. prune: Deletes resources removed from Git. selfHeal: Reverts manual edits. Without these, you have manual GitOps.

📊
Application Health

ArgoCD tracks: Sync Status: Synced / OutOfSync / Unknown. Health Status: Healthy / Progressing / Degraded / Suspended / Missing. Both must be green for production.

📦 Source Types — Four Ways to Define Manifests in ArgoCD

Source TypeHow It WorksBest ForCNPA Relevance
Plain YAMLDirectory of .yaml files. ArgoCD applies them as-is.Simple apps, getting startedWorks but doesn't scale. No environment-specific overrides.
KustomizeBase + overlays pattern. Patches per environment. Native to kubectl.Most teams. anihpj uses this.⭐ CNPA recommended pattern. Simpler than Helm. No templating.
HelmGo templates with values.yaml. Chart dependencies. Hooks.Complex apps, distributing chartsPowerful but harder to debug. CNPA expects you to know it exists.
Jsonnet/KsonnetJSON-based templating language. Programmatic config generation.Large-scale, complex logicMentioned for completeness. Rarely tested.

⚙️ syncOptions Deep Dive — What Each Option Does

OptionEffectWhen to UseRisk
CreateNamespace=trueAuto-creates the target namespace if it doesn't existAlways. Avoids "namespace not found" sync failures.🟢 None
PruneLast=trueDeletes old resources AFTER new ones are healthyAlways with prune. Prevents downtime during rename.🟢 None
PrunePropagationPolicy=foregroundDeletes resources and their dependents before removing from GitCRDs with finalizers. Ensures cleanup completes.🟡 Can block sync if finalizers hang
Validate=trueValidates YAML against K8s API schema before applyingCatch syntax errors before deploy. Default: true.🟢 None
ApplyOutOfSyncOnly=trueOnly sync resources that are OutOfSync (skip synced ones)Large apps — speeds up sync. Avoid redundant applies.🟢 None
RespectIgnoreDifferences=trueHonors ignoreDifferences config during syncWhen you want ArgoCD to ignore certain fields (e.g., HPA currentReplicas)🟡 Can mask real drift
💡 Application vs ApplicationSet

An Application deploys ONE app to ONE cluster. An ApplicationSet generates MULTIPLE Applications from a template using generators (list, cluster, matrix). For the anihpj platform: one ApplicationSet with a list generator [dev, staging, prod] × [jobpost, redis, postgres] creates 9 Applications automatically. Covered in detail in Chapter 16.

15.6 Sync Strategies — Manual, Automated, and Self-Healing

ArgoCD's sync behavior is controlled by the syncPolicy in the Application CRD. The choice between manual sync, automated sync, and self-healing represents a tradeoff between control and automation — and is a key CNPA design decision:

StrategyBehaviorUse CaseRisk Level
Manual SyncArgoCD detects OutOfSync but does NOT apply. Developer clicks "Sync" in UI or runs argocd app sync.Production apps. Every change requires human approval.🟢 Lowest
Automated (no prune/self-heal)ArgoCD auto-applies new/changed resources. Does NOT delete old resources or revert manual edits.Staging. Fast feedback. Low risk of deleting things.🟡 Medium
Automated + PruneArgoCD auto-applies AND deletes resources removed from Git. Manual edits NOT reverted.Dev environments. Clean up old resources automatically.🟠 Higher
Automated + Prune + Self-HealFull GitOps. ArgoCD auto-applies, deletes, AND reverts manual edits. Cluster always = Git.Staging + Dev. NOT recommended for critical prod.🔴 Highest

Self-Heal — The Drift Reverter

Self-heal is what makes GitOps truly "the cluster matches Git." Without it, a manual kubectl edit deployment persists until the next sync. WITH self-heal, ArgoCD detects the drift every 3 minutes and reverts it back to what's in Git:

🩹 SELF-HEAL IN ACTION
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  TIME    EVENT                               CLUSTER STATE           │
│  ────    ─────                               ─────────────           │
│  T=0     Git: replicas=3                     replicas=3 ✅           │
│  T=5m    Admin runs:                          replicas=5 ⚠️          │
│          kubectl scale deploy/anihpj                                  │
│          --replicas=5 (emergency fix)                                 │
│  T=6m    ArgoCD detects:                      replicas=5 ⚠️          │
│          "Desired=3, Actual=5. Drift!"                               │
│          Self-heal triggers:                  replicas=3 ✅           │
│          kubectl scale --replicas=3                                   │
│  T=7m    Cluster back to Git state            replicas=3 ✅           │
│                                                                       │
│  ⚠️  DANGER: Self-heal reverts EMERGENCY fixes too!                  │
│  If you need a hotfix:                                               │
│  • Option A: git commit + auto-sync (GitOps way)                     │
│  • Option B: Pause ArgoCD → kubectl fix → resume ArgoCD              │
│  • Option C: Disable self-heal for production apps                   │
│                                                                       │
│  anihpj policy:                                                      │
│  • Dev: automated + prune + selfHeal (full auto)                     │
│  • Staging: automated + prune (no self-heal — test manual edits)     │
│  • Prod: manual sync only (approval required)                        │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
⚠️ Prune: The Delete Mechanism

When prune: true, ArgoCD DELETES resources that exist in the cluster but NOT in Git. Example: You rename service.yaml to svc.yaml in Git. Without prune, the old Service stays. With prune, the old Service is deleted. This is powerful but dangerous — always use PruneLast=true to ensure new resources are healthy before old ones are removed.

🎯 Sync Strategy Decision Matrix — What to Use Where

EnvironmentSync StrategyPruneSelf-HealRationale
DevAutomated✅ Yes✅ YesFastest feedback. Devs see changes immediately. No manual approval needed. If something breaks, it's dev — no users affected.
StagingAutomated✅ Yes⚠️ OptionalTest auto-sync behavior before prod. Prune keeps staging clean. Self-heal optional — some teams want to test manual edits.
ProductionManual✅ Yes❌ NoHuman approval for every prod change. Prune yes — don't leave orphaned resources. Self-heal NO — emergency hotfixes shouldn't be auto-reverted.
DR ClusterAutomated✅ Yes✅ YesMust mirror production exactly. Full auto-sync ensures DR is always ready. No human in the loop.

⚡ Sync Triggers — Webhook vs Polling

✅ WEBHOOK (Fast)

How: Git provider (GitHub/GitLab) sends HTTP POST to ArgoCD on every push. ArgoCD immediately reconciles.

Latency: ~10-60 seconds from git push to sync

Setup: Configure webhook in GitHub → ArgoCD API Server endpoint

Best for: Production, staging — any environment where you want instant sync

anihpj: Webhook configured for all environments. Push → Auto-sync in < 60s.

⚠️ POLLING (Simple, Default)

How: ArgoCD checks Git every 3 minutes (configurable). Detects new commits on next poll cycle.

Latency: 0-180 seconds (average 90s) from git push to sync

Setup: None — works out of the box. No webhook config needed.

Best for: Dev environments, getting started. No network config needed.

Caveat: Higher latency. Not ideal when every second counts.

💡 When Self-Heal "Bites" — The 2AM Scenario

Production goes down at 2AM. On-call engineer runs kubectl scale deployment/jobpost --replicas=10 to handle traffic. ArgoCD, with selfHeal enabled, reverts it back to 3 replicas within 3 minutes. Production goes down AGAIN. The engineer scales to 10 again. ArgoCD reverts again. This "tug of war" is why selfHeal is disabled in production. The proper GitOps response: pause ArgoCD → apply emergency fix → commit to Git → resume ArgoCD.

15.7 GitOps Repository Structure — Organizing for Scale

As your platform grows, a single flat directory of YAML files becomes unmanageable. The app-of-apps pattern and Kustomize overlays provide the structure needed to manage dozens of applications across multiple environments from a single GitOps repository:

📁 GITOPS REPOSITORY STRUCTURE — App-of-Apps Pattern
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  anihpj-gitops/                                                      │
│  ├── argocd/                         # ArgoCD's own config           │
│  │   └── root-app.yaml              # App-of-Apps root              │
│  │                                                                   │
│  ├── apps/                           # Individual app manifests      │
│  │   ├── anihpj/                                                     │
│  │   │   ├── base/                   # Common Kustomize base         │
│  │   │   │   ├── kustomization.yaml                                 │
│  │   │   │   ├── deployment.yaml     # replicas: 1 (base default)   │
│  │   │   │   ├── service.yaml                                       │
│  │   │   │   └── ingress.yaml                                       │
│  │   │   └── overlays/               # Environment-specific         │
│  │   │       ├── dev/                                                │
│  │   │       │   ├── kustomization.yaml  # replicas: 1, debug: true │
│  │   │       │   └── configmap.yaml                                  │
│  │   │       ├── staging/                                            │
│  │   │       │   ├── kustomization.yaml  # replicas: 2, log: debug  │

Kustomize Overlays — Environment-Specific Config

YAMLapps/anihpj/overlays/prod/kustomization.yaml
apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Kustomization

# Inherit from base
resources:
  - ../../base

# Override replica count for production
patches:
  - patch: |-
      - op: replace
        path: /spec/replicas
        value: 5
    target:
      kind: Deployment
      name: jobpost

# Add production-specific resources
resources:
  - hpa.yaml
  - network-policy.yaml

# Set production namespace
namespace: anihpj-prod

# Common labels for all resources
commonLabels:
  environment: production
  tier: frontend
📖 Repo Structure Best Practices

One repo vs many: Monorepo (all apps in one repo) is simpler for small teams. Multi-repo (one per app) scales better for large orgs. app-of-apps: Always use this pattern. One root Application creates child Applications. Bootstrap once. Kustomize vs Helm: Kustomize is simpler and native to kubectl. Helm has templating (if/else/loops). Both work with ArgoCD. The CNPA exam expects you to know BOTH.

🏗️ Monorepo vs Multi-Repo — Choosing Your Structure

✅ MONOREPO (anihpj's choice)

Structure: ALL apps in ONE Git repo. apps/jobpost/, apps/redis/, apps/postgres/ all together.

Pros: One PR can change multiple apps atomically. Single source of truth. Easier discovery. Consistent Kustomize base.

Cons: Repo grows large. CI needs to handle monorepo scale. Permissions are all-or-nothing (can't restrict Redis team from seeing JobPost config).

Best for: Small-medium teams (<50 engineers). Tightly coupled microservices. Platform engineering teams.

⚠️ MULTI-REPO (Alternative)

Structure: ONE repo per app. github.com/anihpj/jobpost-gitops, github.com/anihpj/redis-gitops.

Pros: Independent permissions per app. Smaller, faster clones. Teams own their repos. Independent CI.

Cons: Cross-cutting changes require multiple PRs. Harder to discover all apps. Inconsistent patterns across repos.

Best for: Large orgs (>100 engineers). Independent product teams. Strict compliance boundaries.

🚫 Common GitOps Anti-Patterns — What NOT to Do

The CNPA exam tests your ability to spot broken GitOps implementations. Here are the most common mistakes teams make — and the correct GitOps approach for each:

🚫
❌ Git + kubectl = GitOps

"I store my YAML in Git and run kubectl apply from my laptop." This is configuration management, not GitOps. Missing: automated pull (P3) and continuous reconciliation (P4). The agent must run INSIDE the cluster and pull automatically.

🚫
❌ CI Push with KUBECONFIG = GitOps

"My CI pipeline runs kubectl apply after every build — that's GitOps, right?" WRONG. This is push-based CD. The CI system stores cluster credentials externally (security risk). There's no continuous reconciliation — drift persists until the next pipeline run.

🚫
❌ No Pruning — Orphaned Resources

You rename api-service.yaml to api-svc.yaml in Git. Without prune: true, the old Service object remains in the cluster forever. Over months, dozens of orphaned resources accumulate. Fix: enable prune in syncPolicy.

🚫
❌ Self-Heal in Production

Production goes down at 2AM. On-call engineer scales up replicas manually. ArgoCD self-heal reverts it. Engineer scales again. ArgoCD reverts again. This "tug of war" blocks emergency response. Fix: manual sync for production, self-heal only for dev.

🚫
❌ One Giant Flat Directory

All 200 YAML files in /manifests/. No separation by app or environment. Nobody knows which file belongs to which service. Fix: organize by app with Kustomize overlays — apps/{name}/base/ + apps/{name}/overlays/{env}/.

🚫
❌ Environment Branches in Git

Branch dev, staging, prod with different YAML per branch. Cherry-picking between branches. Merge conflicts on config changes. Fix: ONE branch (main) with Kustomize overlays per environment. Environment = directory, not branch.

⚠️ The Golden Rule of GitOps

If you need cluster credentials OUTSIDE the cluster, it's NOT GitOps. The agent must run inside the cluster. The cluster pulls from Git — Git never pushes to the cluster. This single rule eliminates 90% of "fake GitOps" implementations. Remember: Pull + In-Cluster = GitOps. Push + External = NOT GitOps.

🔐 The Secrets Problem — "How Do I Store Passwords in Git?"

This is the #1 question teams ask when adopting GitOps: "If all config is in Git, where do I put database passwords, API keys, and TLS certificates?" The answer is NOT "put plaintext secrets in Git" — that's a security disaster. Instead, GitOps uses encryption tools that let you store ENCRYPTED secrets in Git safely. Only the cluster (via a controller) can decrypt them:

🔒
Sealed Secrets

How: A controller in the cluster generates a public/private key pair. You encrypt secrets client-side with kubeseal using the public key. The encrypted SealedSecret is safe to store in Git. Only the controller (with the private key) can decrypt it into a regular K8s Secret.

Best for: Simple setups. GitOps-native. No external dependencies. anihpj uses this for staging.

🔑
External Secrets Operator (ESO)

How: Secrets NEVER touch Git. ESO syncs secrets from external providers (AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, HashiCorp Vault, GCP Secret Manager) into K8s Secrets automatically. You define an ExternalSecret CR that says "get secret X from AWS, put it in K8s Secret Y."

Best for: Enterprise. Centralized secret management. Compliance (secrets never in Git at all). anihpj uses this for production.

🔐
SOPS + Age/GPG

How: Mozilla SOPS encrypts entire YAML/JSON files (not just values). Encryption keys managed by Age or GPG. Encrypted files are stored in Git safely. ArgoCD can decrypt SOPS files natively via a plugin.

Best for: Teams already using SOPS. Encrypting entire config files (not just individual secrets). Flux CD uses SOPS natively.

📖 The Secret Management Decision

Sealed Secrets: Simple, GitOps-native, but secrets ARE in Git (encrypted). ESO: Secrets NEVER in Git, centralized management, but requires external secret store. SOPS: Flexible, encrypts whole files, but requires key management. CNPA exam tip: The exam expects you to know that plaintext secrets should NEVER be in Git, and to recognize Sealed Secrets + ESO as the two primary solutions. Detailed coverage in Chapter 16.

15.8 Practice Lab — 10 CNPA Exam-Style Questions

Test your understanding of GitOps principles, ArgoCD architecture, sync strategies, and repository structure. Each question targets a specific exam objective.

Domain 3Q1

What is the defining characteristic that distinguishes GitOps from traditional CI/CD deployment?

A The desired state is stored in Git, and an agent inside the cluster pulls and reconciles it
B The CI pipeline runs kubectl apply against the cluster after building images
C A developer manually syncs manifests from a Git repository to the cluster
D Using Git instead of SVN for version control of Kubernetes manifests

✅ Correct: A

GitOps is defined by pull-based reconciliation: the agent runs INSIDE the cluster, watches a Git repo, and automatically reconciles the actual state to match the desired state in Git. Option B describes the push model. Option C is manual (not automated). Option D is just version control — not GitOps.

Domain 3Q2

Which of the following is NOT one of Weaveworks' four GitOps principles?

A The system must be described declaratively
B The desired state must be versioned and immutable
C All deployments must use Helm charts for templating
D Software agents continuously reconcile actual state toward desired state

✅ Correct: C

The four principles are: Declarative, Versioned & Immutable, Pulled Automatically, and Continuously Reconciled. Helm is ONE way to declare state, but it's not a required principle. Plain YAML, Kustomize, and Jsonnet are equally valid.

Domain 3Q3

The anihpj platform team is transitioning from push-based deployment (GitHub Actions runs kubectl apply) to GitOps with ArgoCD. What is the PRIMARY security benefit of this migration?

A ArgoCD encrypts all YAML manifests at rest in the Git repository
B Cluster credentials no longer need to be stored in the external CI system
C ArgoCD automatically rotates all Kubernetes secrets every 90 days
D Git commits are cryptographically signed, preventing supply chain attacks

✅ Correct: B

In push-based CI/CD, the CI system stores the kubeconfig/credentials to push to the cluster — this is an external attack vector. In GitOps (pull), ArgoCD runs INSIDE the cluster and pulls from Git. No external system needs cluster admin credentials. This is the #1 security advantage of GitOps.

Domain 3Q4

In ArgoCD, which component is responsible for cloning Git repositories and generating manifests from Helm charts or Kustomize overlays?

A API Server
B Application Controller
C Repository Server
D Redis Cache

✅ Correct: C

The Repository Server clones repos, caches them, and generates manifests (Helm, Kustomize, plain YAML). The Application Controller reads the generated manifests and compares them to the cluster state. The API Server exposes the UI and CLI.

Domain 3Q5

In the ArgoCD Application CRD, which of the following correctly identifies the two required specification sections?

A source and health
B repository and namespace
C source and destination
D gitRepo and targetCluster

✅ Correct: C

The Application CRD's spec has source (which Git repo, path, revision) and destination (which cluster server URL and namespace). These are the only two required sections. syncPolicy is optional.

Domain 3Q6

An administrator runs kubectl scale deployment/anihpj --replicas=10 on the production cluster to handle a traffic spike. The Git repo specifies replicas=3. With ArgoCD self-heal enabled, what happens?

A ArgoCD updates the Git repo to replicas=10 to match the cluster
B ArgoCD marks the application as OutOfSync and sends an alert, but takes no action
C ArgoCD detects the drift and scales the deployment back to 3 replicas within the next reconciliation cycle
D ArgoCD merges the values and scales to 6 replicas (average of 3 and 10)

✅ Correct: C

Self-heal means ArgoCD continuously enforces Git as the truth. The manual scale to 10 is treated as drift — ArgoCD reverts it back to 3. This is why self-heal is often DISABLED for production: emergency fixes get reverted. The proper GitOps way is to git commit the replicas change and let ArgoCD sync it.

Domain 3Q7

The anihpj team wants ArgoCD to automatically apply changes from Git AND delete resources that were removed from Git manifests. Which sync policy configuration should they use?

A automated: {} with no additional options
B automated: { prune: true, selfHeal: false }
C automated: { prune: false, selfHeal: true }
D syncPolicy: { whenDeleted: prune }

✅ Correct: B

prune: true removes cluster resources that no longer exist in Git. selfHeal: false means manual edits are NOT automatically reverted. Option A applies new resources but never deletes old ones. Option C reverts manual edits but doesn't delete removed resources. Option D is not a valid ArgoCD field.

Domain 3Q8

What is the purpose of the "app-of-apps" pattern in ArgoCD?

A To deploy multiple container images within a single Kubernetes Deployment
B To run multiple instances of ArgoCD for high availability
C To use one root Application that creates and manages child Applications, enabling bootstrapping of the entire cluster from a single resource
D To group applications by programming language in the ArgoCD UI

✅ Correct: C

The app-of-apps pattern means one root ArgoCD Application creates many child Applications. This is the standard bootstrapping pattern: install ArgoCD → create ONE root app → ArgoCD discovers and manages all child apps. No manual creation of individual Application CRs.

Domain 3Q9

In the anihpj GitOps repository, the base deployment.yaml specifies replicas: 1. The production Kustomize overlay patches it to replicas: 5. What is this pattern called?

A Helm values templating
B Kustomize overlay with strategic merge patch
C Git branching strategy per environment
D ConfigMap generator override

✅ Correct: B

Kustomize uses a base + overlays pattern. The base contains common configuration. Each overlay (dev/staging/prod) patches the base with environment-specific overrides. This is the recommended pattern for environment-specific configurations in GitOps. Helm uses a different approach (values.yaml + templates).

Domain 3Q10

The anihpj platform team wants to deploy the same application to dev, staging, and production Kubernetes clusters from a single GitOps repository. Which ArgoCD feature should they use?

A Create three separate ArgoCD installations, one per cluster
B Use ArgoCD ApplicationSet with a list or matrix generator targeting each cluster
C Use ArgoCD ApplicationSet with a list or matrix generator to create per-cluster Applications
D Copy the YAML manifests into three separate Git branches

✅ Correct: C

ArgoCD ApplicationSet is the feature for multi-cluster deployments. It can generate multiple Application CRs from a template using generators (list, cluster, matrix). For example, a list generator with [dev, staging, prod] × [anihpj, redis] creates 6 Applications. This is the standard approach for GitOps at scale. Option B is close but "list or matrix generator" was worded correctly in C. The key concept is ApplicationSet.
