Safe cleanup

💭 Think Like an Operator — The Reconcile Mindset

Writing an operator forces you to think differently. Instead of writing scripts that say "do this, then that," you write a RECONCILE FUNCTION that asks: "What SHOULD exist? What DOES exist? What's the DIFFERENCE?" — and then makes reality match desire. This shift in thinking is what separates platform engineers from sysadmins:

❌ SCRIPT MINDSET (Imperative)

"Create Deployment. Then create Service. Then create Ingress. If any fail, stop and print error."

Problems: If step 2 fails, step 1 remains. No retry. No cleanup. Fragile. Depends on execution order. Cannot recover from partial failure automatically.

✅ OPERATOR MINDSET (Declarative / Reconcile)

"Ensure Deployment exists with these specs. Ensure Service exists. Ensure Ingress exists. Independently. Forever."

Benefits: Each check is independent. If Service creation fails today, it retries on next reconcile. Deployment is already running. Order doesn't matter. Safe to re-run infinitely.

20.2 Operator Capabilities — Day 0, Day 1, Day 2

What separates an Operator from a simple controller is the scope of its responsibility. An Operator manages the full lifecycle of an application, from creation to deletion. The industry categorizes these responsibilities into three "Days" — a framework that originated from traditional IT operations but applies perfectly to Kubernetes Operators:

📅 OPERATOR LIFECYCLE — Day 0, Day 1, Day 2
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  THE THREE DAYS OF AN APPLICATION — And How an Operator Automates All │
│                                                                       │
│  DAY 0 — PROVISION & INSTALL (The "Birth" of the Application)        │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  "Make the application EXIST"                                    │ │
│  │                                                                  │ │
│  │  WITHOUT Operator (Human does this):                             │ │
│  │  → Read installation guide (23 pages)                            │ │
│  │  → Create namespace, RBAC, ServiceAccounts                      │ │
│  │  → Create ConfigMaps with config values                         │ │
│  │  → Create Secrets with credentials                              │ │
│  │  → Create StatefulSet/Deployment with correct image             │ │
│  │  → Create Service, Ingress, PVC                                 │ │
│  │  → Initialize database schema, run migrations                   │ │
│  │  → Configure monitoring, logging, alerting                      │ │
│  │  → Time: 2-4 hours. Error-prone. Inconsistent.                  │ │
│  │                                                                  │ │
│  │  WITH Operator (Operator does this):                             │ │
│  │  → $ kubectl apply -f anihpj-jobboard.yaml                      │ │
│  │  → Operator creates ALL resources automatically                  │ │
│  │  → Operator runs database migrations                            │ │
│  │  → Operator waits for health checks to pass                     │ │
│  │  → Operator updates status: "Ready"                              │ │
│  │  → Time: 5-10 minutes. Consistent. Repeatable.                  │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                       │
│  DAY 1 — CONFIGURE & UPDATE (The "Growth" of the Application)         │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  "Change the application's configuration while it's running"     │ │
│  │                                                                  │ │
│  │  WITHOUT Operator:                                               │ │
│  │  → Edit ConfigMap manually (kubectl edit)                        │ │
│  │  → Restart pods one at a time (kubectl rollout restart)          │ │
│  │  → Verify each pod comes back healthy                            │ │
│  │  → Roll back if something breaks                                 │ │
│  │  → Update runbook with new procedure                             │ │
│  │                                                                  │ │
│  │  WITH Operator:                                                  │ │
│  │  → Developer updates JobBoard spec: replicas 3→5, image v2.1→v2.2│ │
│  │  → Operator detects change                                      │ │
│  │  → Operator performs ROLLING UPDATE (one pod at a time)         │ │
│  │  → Operator monitors health during rollout                      │ │
│  │  → Operator pauses if health checks fail                        │ │
│  │  → Operator AUTO-ROLLBACKS if deployment fails                  │ │
│  │  → Zero downtime. Zero human intervention.                      │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                       │
│  DAY 2 — HEAL, SCALE, BACKUP (The "Life" of the Application)          │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  "Keep the application healthy, 24/7/365"                        │ │
│  │  THIS IS WHERE OPERATORS PROVIDE THE MOST VALUE                 │ │
│  │                                                                  │ │
│  │  AUTO-HEALING:                                                   │ │
│  │  • Pod crashes → Operator recreates it                           │ │
│  │  • Node fails → Operator reschedules pods                       │ │
│  │  • Database primary fails → Operator FAILOVERS to standby       │ │
│  │  • Disk fills up → Operator triggers auto-resize                │ │
│  │  • Certificate expiring → Operator requests new cert            │ │
│  │                                                                  │ │
│  │  AUTO-SCALING:                                                   │ │
│  │  • CPU > 80% → Operator scales from 3→5 replicas                │ │
│  │  • Memory pressure → Operator increases resource requests       │ │
│  │  • Storage approaching limit → Operator expands PVC             │ │
│  │                                                                  │ │
│  │  AUTO-BACKUP:                                                    │ │
│  │  • Every 6 hours → Operator takes PostgreSQL snapshot            │ │
│  │  • Every midnight → Operator runs pg_dump to S3                 │ │
│  │  • Retention: 7 daily + 4 weekly + 12 monthly                   │ │
│  │                                                                  │ │
│  │  AUTO-MONITORING:                                                │ │
│  │  • Operator exposes /metrics endpoint                            │ │
│  │  • Prometheus scrapes: replication lag, connection count,        │ │
│  │    query performance, disk usage, backup status                  │ │
│  │  • Operator writes status conditions to CR                       │ │
│  │  • Alertmanager fires if operator detects issues                │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                       │
│  THE KEY INSIGHT: Day 2 is where Operators truly shine.               │
│  • A simple script can do Day 0 (provision).                         │
│  • A CI/CD pipeline can do Day 1 (deploy).                            │
│  • ONLY an Operator can do Day 2 CONTINUOUSLY, 24/7, automatically.  │
│  • The operator NEVER stops. It's always watching. Always healing.   │

LevelCapabilityExample
Phase I: Basic InstallAutomated Day 0 — creates resources from CRMost Helm-based operators (install, configure, done)
Phase II: Seamless UpgradesDay 1 — rolling updates, version upgrades, rollbackPostgres Operator: upgrade from PG 14 → 15 with zero downtime
Phase III: Full LifecycleDay 2 — backup, restore, failover, scaling, monitoringStrimzi Kafka: auto-rebalance partitions on scale-up

🔧 Day 2 in Practice — What Your Operator Should Actually Do

Day 2 operations aren't theoretical. Here's a concrete checklist of what a production-grade Operator should handle — and how it should handle each scenario:

🔧 DAY 2 OPERATIONS — The Production Operator Checklist
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  DAY 2 PRODUCTION CHECKLIST — What Your Operator Must Handle          │
│                                                                       │
│  ☐ POD CRASHES — Auto-Healing                                        │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Pod OOMKilled → Operator detects NotReady status               │ │
│  │  → If StatefulSet: checks pod ordinal, restarts same pod        │ │
│  │  → If Deployment: lets ReplicaSet handle replacement            │ │
│  │  → Logs event: "Pod crash detected: OOMKilled on worker-3"      │ │
│  │  → Updates CR status: "1 pod crashed, auto-recovering..."       │ │
│  │  → ⚠️  If same pod crashes 3+ times in 10 minutes → alert!     │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                       │
│  ☐ STORAGE FULL — Auto-Expansion                                     │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  PVC usage > 80% → Operator checks if volume expansion enabled  │ │
│  │  → If yes: patches PVC to larger size (20Gi → 40Gi)             │ │
│  │  → Then: restarts pod gracefully (filesystem resize needs it)   │ │
│  │  → If no: creates alert, updates CR status: "Disk nearly full"  │ │
│  │  → ⚠️  Never expand beyond max limit (spec.maxStorage)          │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                       │
│  ☐ CERTIFICATE EXPIRING — Auto-Renewal                               │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  TLS cert expires in < 7 days → Operator requests new cert      │ │
│  │  → Updates Secret with new cert                                 │ │
│  │  → Triggers rolling restart to pick up new cert                 │ │
│  │  → Updates CR status: "Certificate renewed, valid until..."     │ │
│  │  → ⚠️  Don't restart ALL pods at once (rolling, 1 at a time)   │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                       │
│  ☐ DATABASE FAILOVER — Automated                                     │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Primary pod NotReady > 30s → Operator checks standby status    │ │
│  │  → Standby is healthy AND replication lag < 5s → PROMOTE       │ │
│  │  → Updates Service to point to new primary                      │ │
│  │  → Creates replacement standby pod                               │ │
│  │  → Updates CR status: "Failover completed at 03:02:15 UTC"      │ │
│  │  → ⚠️  Never failover if replication lag > 5s (data loss!)     │ │
│  │  → ⚠️  Never failover if split-brain detected                  │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                       │
│  ☐ VERSION UPGRADE — Rolling with Health Checks                      │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  User updates CR: spec.version: "15" → "16"                      │ │
│  │  → Operator validates: is this a supported upgrade path?        │ │
│  │  → Runs pg_upgrade --check FIRST (dry run)                      │ │
│  │  → If check passes → begins rolling upgrade:                     │ │
│  │    → Upgrade standby-1 → wait for healthy → upgrade standby-2   │ │
│  │    → Switchover: promote standby → upgrade old primary          │ │
│  │  → If ANY step fails → ROLLBACK to v15, update CR status        │ │
│  │  → ⚠️  Always take a backup BEFORE upgrading                   │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                       │
│  ☐ SCHEDULED BACKUPS — Never Miss One                                 │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  CR spec: {backup: {schedule: "0 */6 * * *", retention: 30}}   │ │
│  │  → Operator creates CronJob (or internal scheduler)              │ │
│  │  → Every 6 hours: pg_dump → compress → upload to S3             │ │
│  │  → Verifies backup integrity (restore to temp pod, check)       │ │
│  │  → Cleans up backups older than retention (30 days)              │ │
│  │  → Updates CR status: "Last backup: 2026-06-21 06:00 UTC, OK"  │ │
│  │  → ⚠️  If backup fails → update status → alert immediately     │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

🌐 Network Partitions & The CAP Theorem — What Every Operator Author Must Know

Operators run in distributed systems. Distributed systems experience network partitions — where pods can't talk to each other but are still running. An Operator that doesn't handle partitions correctly will CORRUPT DATA. Here's what you must understand:

🌐 OPERATORS AND THE CAP THEOREM — Choosing Consistency vs Availability
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  THE CAP THEOREM AND OPERATORS — A Practical Guide                    │
│                                                                       │
│  THE CAP THEOREM: You can only have TWO of {Consistency, Availability,│
│  Partition Tolerance} simultaneously. Since networks ALWAYS partition │
│  eventually, every operator must choose: CP or AP?                   │
│                                                                       │
│  SCENARIO: PostgreSQL Operator, 3-node cluster (primary + 2 standbys) │
│                                                                       │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │              NORMAL OPERATION                                    │ │
│  │                                                                  │ │
│  │  ┌──────────┐     ┌──────────┐     ┌──────────┐                │ │
│  │  │ PRIMARY  │────▶│ STANDBY-1│────▶│ STANDBY-2│                │ │
│  │  │ (writes) │     │ (replica)│     │ (replica)│                │ │
│  │  └──────────┘     └──────────┘     └──────────┘                │ │
│  │  Zone: us-east-1a  Zone: us-east-1b  Zone: us-east-1c          │ │
│  │                                                                  │ │
│  │  All nodes connected. Replication flowing. Everything healthy.  │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                       │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │              NETWORK PARTITION (us-east-1c isolated!)            │ │
│  │                                                                  │ │
│  │  ┌──────────┐     ┌──────────┐          ┌──────────┐           │ │
│  │  │ PRIMARY  │────▶│ STANDBY-1│    ❌    │ STANDBY-2│           │ │
│  │  │ (writes) │     │ (replica)│    ╳─────│ (ISOLATED)│           │ │
│  │  └──────────┘     └──────────┘          └──────────┘           │ │
│  │  Zone: us-east-1a  Zone: us-east-1b     Zone: us-east-1c       │ │
│  │                                                                  │ │
│  │  WHAT SHOULD THE OPERATOR DO?                                     │ │
│  │                                                                  │ │
│  │  CHOICE A: CP — CONSISTENCY OVER AVAILABILITY                    │ │
│  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐│ │
│  │  │ "Data integrity is everything. Never risk data loss."       ││ │
│  │  │                                                              ││ │
│  │  │  Operator action:                                            ││ │
│  │  │  1. Operator detects STANDBY-2 is unreachable               ││ │
│  │  │  2. Operator does NOT promote STANDBY-2 (split-brain danger)││ │
│  │  │  3. Operator continues accepting writes on PRIMARY          ││ │
│  │  │  4. Operator alerts: "STANDBY-2 unreachable — investigate"  ││ │
│  │  │  5. If PRIMARY goes down in the partition → SERVICE STOPS   ││ │
│  │  │     (sacrificing availability for consistency)              ││ │
│  │  │                                                              ││ │
│  │  │  Used by: PostgreSQL, etcd, Zookeeper (CP systems)          ││ │
│  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘│ │
│  │                                                                  │ │
│  │  CHOICE B: AP — AVAILABILITY OVER CONSISTENCY                    │ │
│  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐│ │
│  │  │ "The service must stay up. Reconcile conflicts later."      ││ │
│  │  │                                                              ││ │
│  │  │  Operator action:                                            ││ │
│  │  │  1. Operator detects STANDBY-2 is isolated                   ││ │
│  │  │  2. Operator promotes STANDBY-2 to PRIMARY (local writes)   ││ │
│  │  │  3. BOTH sides accept writes → DATA DIVERGES                ││ │
│  │  │  4. When partition heals → Operator detects CONFLICT        ││ │
│  │  │  5. Operator applies conflict resolution (last-write-wins,  ││ │
│  │  │     CRDT merge, or manual intervention)                     ││ │
│  │  │  6. SERVICE NEVER STOPS (sacrificing consistency)           ││ │
│  │  │                                                              ││ │
│  │  │  Used by: Cassandra, Riak, DynamoDB (AP systems)            ││ │
│  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘│ │
│  │                                                                  │ │
│  │  THE CNPA RULE:                                                   │ │
│  │  • Financial data → CP (never lose a transaction)                │ │
│  │  • Social media feeds → AP (show something, even if slightly    │ │
│  │    stale, rather than "service unavailable")                    │ │
│  │  • Your Operator MUST document its CAP choice                   │ │
│  │  • NEVER try to have both — that's physically impossible        │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                       │
│  HOW OPERATORS DETECT NETWORK PARTITIONS:                              │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  • Lease expiry: If leader can't renew its Lease (check 20.1),  │ │
│  │    it knows it might be partitioned from the API server         │ │
│  │  • Peer health checks: Operator checks other pods via their     │ │
│  │    /healthz endpoints (not via K8s API — direct pod-to-pod)     │ │
│  │  • Quorum: "Can I reach > 50% of my peers?" If yes → I'm in    │ │
│  │    the majority partition → I can act. If no → I'm isolated.    │ │
│  │  • Fencing tokens: etcd uses Raft term numbers. If I'm term 5  │ │
│  │    but someone claims to be term 6 → I'm stale, step down.     │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

⚠️ Real Operator Failure Modes — What the CNPA Exam Tests

Operators are software, and software has bugs. Understanding HOW operators fail is as important as understanding how they succeed:

❌ The Cascading Recreate Loop
  • Symptom: Operator fixes a "problem," but the fix creates a NEW problem that triggers another reconcile. Loop forever.
  • Real example: Operator set wrong label on a pod → next reconcile detected "pod doesn't have correct label" → deleted pod → recreated with SAME wrong label → infinite delete-recreate. Pods churned every 10 seconds for hours.
  • Fix: The reconcile function must be STABLE — running it twice must produce the same result as running it once. If reconcile output differs from input, you have a bug.
❌ The Orphaned Cloud Resources
  • Symptom: CR deleted. K8s removes the CR. But the RDS database, S3 bucket, and DNS record remain — costing money every month.
  • Real example: Finalizer code had a bug. API call to delete RDS timed out. Operator returned error. On next reconcile, the CR was already gone (deleted), so the finalizer never executed. $1,200/month RDS instance ran for 6 months until found during cost audit.
  • Fix: Finalizers must handle partial failures. Retry with backoff. Log WARNINGS when cleanup fails. Consider a separate garbage-collector controller.
✅ Mitigated: The Split-Brain Database (How CloudNativePG Prevents It)
  • The Risk: Network partition isolates primary. Operator in isolated zone promotes standby. BOTH sides accept writes. Data diverges.
  • CloudNativePG's Prevention: (1) Kubernetes leases with strict timeouts. (2) Requires QUORUM (>50% of pods reachable) before any failover. (3) Generation numbers — highest generation wins when partition heals. (4) Isolated pod writes are rejected on rejoin.
  • Lesson: THIS is why you ADOPT CloudNativePG instead of BUILDING your own database operator. These edge cases took YEARS to discover and fix across thousands of production clusters.

20.3 Operator SDK Frameworks — Choosing Your Weapon

You don't write an Operator entirely from scratch. Four major frameworks provide the scaffolding, the controller-runtime machinery (from 20.1), and the project structure. Choosing the right one depends on your team's language expertise, the complexity of your operator's logic, and whether you're managing stateless or stateful workloads:

🔷
Kubebuilder (Go)

Most popular. CNCF & K8s SIG standard. Used by Prometheus Operator, cert-manager, Cluster API, and Crossplane. Generates Go project structure with controller-runtime. Best for: Complex stateful operators, production-grade platforms, teams with Go expertise.

🔴
Operator SDK (Go/Helm/Ansible)

Red Hat's framework. Supports THREE development approaches: Go-based (like Kubebuilder), Helm-based (wrap existing Helm charts), and Ansible-based (use Ansible playbooks as reconcile logic). Best for: Organizations already using Ansible, simple stateless operators, Helm chart conversion.

🐍
Kopf (Python)

Pythonic operator framework. Handlers are Python async functions decorated with @kopf.on.create, @kopf.on.update. Auto-generates CRD schemas from Python data classes. Best for: Python teams (like anihpj!), rapid prototyping, AI/ML operators, data pipeline operators.

☕
Java Operator SDK

JVM ecosystem. Built on the same controller-runtime principles. Integrates with Spring Boot, Quarkus, and Micronaut. Best for: Java/Spring organizations, Kafka/Strimzi-style operators, enterprise JVM platforms.

📊 Framework Comparison — Decision Matrix
