│  │    → Output: "🔓 Logged in as @developer (team-payments)"        │ │
│  │                                                                   │ │
│  │  anihpj-cli whoami                                                │ │
│  │    → Shows current user + team + RBAC permissions                │ │
│  │    → Output: "@developer | Team: payments | Can: deploy, logs"   │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

🛠️ Building the CLI — Implementation Pattern

The CLI doesn't contain platform logic — it's a thin wrapper that calls platform APIs. This architecture keeps the CLI simple, makes it easy to add a web UI later (they both call the same APIs), and ensures consistency (the CLI can't do anything the portal can't):

Python — anihpj-cli Implementation (Click + requests) 
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# anihpj-cli — Platform CLI (Python + Click)
# Architecture: CLI → Platform API → Backend Services
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

import click
import requests
from pathlib import Path
import json

API_BASE = "https://platform-api.anihpj.io"
CONFIG_DIR = Path.home() / ".anihpj"
TOKEN_FILE = CONFIG_DIR / "token"

def get_auth_header():
    """Read saved OAuth token."""
    if TOKEN_FILE.exists():
        return {"Authorization": f"Bearer {TOKEN_FILE.read_text().strip()}"}
    return {}

@click.group()
def cli():
    """anihpj — Internal Developer Platform CLI"""
    pass

# ─── LOGIN: Authenticate with the platform ───
@cli.command()
@click.option("--sso", default="github", help="SSO provider")
def login(sso):
    """Log in to the anihpj platform."""
    click.echo(f"Opening browser for {sso} authentication...")
    # OAuth2 device flow: open browser, user approves, poll for token
    import webbrowser
    webbrowser.open(f"{API_BASE}/auth/{sso}/login")
    token = click.prompt("Enter token from browser", hide_input=True)
    CONFIG_DIR.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    TOKEN_FILE.write_text(token)
    # Fetch user info
    resp = requests.get(f"{API_BASE}/api/v1/whoami", headers=get_auth_header())
    if resp.ok:
        user = resp.json()
        click.echo(f"🔓 Logged in as {user['username']} (Team: {user['team']})")
    else:
        click.echo("❌ Authentication failed", err=True)

# ─── CREATE SERVICE: Scaffold via Backstage API ───
@cli.command()
@click.argument("name")
@click.option("--team", required=True, help="Team that owns this service")
@click.option("--template", default="django-service", help="Software Template to use")
@click.option("--description", default="", help="Brief description")
def create_service(name, team, template, description):
    """Scaffold a new service from a Software Template."""
    click.echo(f"🏗️  Scaffolding service '{name}' using template '{template}'...")
    resp = requests.post(
        f"{API_BASE}/api/scaffolder/v2/tasks",
        headers={**get_auth_header(), "Content-Type": "application/json"},
        json={
            "templateName": template,
            "values": {
                "name": name,
                "owner": team,
                "description": description,
            }
        }
    )
    if resp.ok:
        task = resp.json()
        click.echo(f"✅ Created! Task ID: {task['id']}")
        click.echo(f"   Repo: https://github.com/anihpj/{name}")
        click.echo(f"   Track progress: anihpj-cli status {name}")
    else:
        click.echo(f"❌ Failed: {resp.json().get('error', resp.text)}", err=True)

# ─── STATUS: Query ArgoCD + K8s for service health ───
@cli.command()
@click.argument("service")
def status(service):
    """Show deployment status of a service."""
    # Query ArgoCD API
    argocd_resp = requests.get(
        f"{API_BASE}/api/argocd/applications/{service}",
        headers=get_auth_header()
    )
    if not argocd_resp.ok:
        click.echo(f"❌ Service '{service}' not found", err=True)
        return

    app = argocd_resp.json()
    sync_status = app['status']['sync']['status']  # Synced, OutOfSync
    health_status = app['status']['health']['status']  # Healthy, Degraded

    # Map to emoji
    sync_icon = {"Synced": "✅", "OutOfSync": "🔄"}.get(sync_status, "❓")
    health_icon = {"Healthy": "💚", "Degraded": "⚠️", "Missing": "❌"}.get(health_status, "❓")

    click.echo(f"📊 {service}")
    click.echo(f"   {sync_icon} Sync: {sync_status}")
    click.echo(f"   {health_icon} Health: {health_status}")
    click.echo(f"   🔗 ArgoCD: https://argocd.anihpj.io/applications/{service}")
    click.echo(f"   🌐 Backstage: https://backstage.anihpj.io/catalog/default/component/{service}")

# ─── LOGS: Query Loki for service logs ───
@cli.command()
@click.argument("service")
@click.option("--tail", default=100, help="Number of log lines")
@click.option("--since", default="1h", help="Time range (1h, 30m, 24h)")
def logs(service, tail, since):
    """View recent logs for a service."""
    click.echo(f"📜 Fetching last {tail} log lines for {service} (since {since})...")
    resp = requests.get(
        f"{API_BASE}/api/loki/query_range",
        headers=get_auth_header(),
        params={
            "query": f'{{app="{service}"}}',
            "limit": tail,
            "since": since,
        }
    )
    if resp.ok:
        data = resp.json()
        for entry in data.get('result', []):
            timestamp = entry['timestamp']
            line = entry['line']
            # Colorize based on log level
            if 'ERROR' in line:
                click.echo(f"{timestamp} 🔴 {line}")
            elif 'WARN' in line:
                click.echo(f"{timestamp} 🟡 {line}")
            else:
                click.echo(f"{timestamp}   {line}")
    else:
        click.echo("❌ Failed to fetch logs", err=True)

# ─── DEPLOY: Trigger deployment (update image tag in Git) ───
@cli.command()
@click.argument("service")
@click.option("--env", default="staging", type=click.Choice(["staging", "production"]))
@click.option("--version", help="Version to deploy (default: latest main)")
def deploy(service, env, version):
    """Deploy a service to an environment."""
    click.echo(f"🚀 Deploying {service} to {env}...")
    resp = requests.post(
        f"{API_BASE}/api/cd/deploy",
        headers={**get_auth_header(), "Content-Type": "application/json"},
        json={"service": service, "environment": env, "version": version}
    )
    if resp.ok:
        result = resp.json()
        click.echo(f"✅ Deployment triggered! ArgoCD syncing...")
        click.echo(f"   Track: anihpj-cli status {service}")
    else:
        click.echo(f"❌ Deployment failed: {resp.json().get('error')}", err=True)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    cli()

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# CLI DESIGN PRINCIPLES:
# 1. THIN WRAPPER: CLI calls Platform API → API calls services.
#    The CLI has NO business logic. Zero. Just HTTP calls.
# 2. SELF-DOCUMENTING: --help should be sufficient.
#    anihpj-cli create service --help → shows all options.
# 3. CONSISTENT OUTPUT: Every command returns structured output
#    (JSON when piped, human-readable when terminal).
# 4. AUTHENTICATED: Single login → all commands use the token.
#    Same token works for CLI and portal (single identity).
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
📖 CLI vs Portal — When Developers Use Which

Portal (Backstage): Discovery ("what services exist?"), documentation (TechDocs), service creation (Scaffolder), dependency visualization. Best for exploring, learning, and one-time setup tasks.
CLI (anihpj-cli): Daily operations (deploy, logs, status), scripting (CI/CD pipelines), power users (bulk operations). Best for repetitive tasks and automation.
Both call the same Platform API — the CLI is just a terminal-friendly wrapper around the same endpoints the portal uses. A developer can create a service in the portal, then manage it from the CLI, and the experience is consistent.

📋 CLI Output Formats — Human-Readable AND Machine-Readable

A well-designed CLI produces output in multiple formats depending on context. When a human is reading the output in a terminal, it should be colorful, formatted, and scannable. When the output is piped to another command or used in a CI script, it should be structured JSON. The same command should serve both use cases:

Shell — CLI Output Formats: Human vs Machine 
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# HUMAN OUTPUT (terminal, default) — colorful, formatted
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

$ anihpj-cli status payments

📊 Service: payments
   ✅ Sync: Synced (commit abc1234)
   💚 Health: Healthy (3/3 pods)
   🔗 ArgoCD: https://argocd.anihpj.io/applications/payments
   🌐 Backstage: https://backstage.anihpj.io/catalog/default/component/payments
   📊 Dashboard: https://grafana.anihpj.io/d/payments-health

$ anihpj-cli status payments --output json

{
  "service": "payments",
  "sync": {
    "status": "Synced",
    "commit": "abc1234"
  },
  "health": {
    "status": "Healthy",
    "readyReplicas": 3,
    "desiredReplicas": 3
  },

    "backstage": "https://backstage.anihpj.io/catalog/default/component/payments",

  }
}

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

$ anihpj-cli status payments --output json | jq -r '.health.readyReplicas'

$ anihpj-cli status payments --output json | jq -r '.sync.commit'
abc1234

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# BULK OPERATIONS — Query all services in a team
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

$ anihpj-cli status --team payments --output json | jq '.[] | {name: .service, healthy: .health.status}'
{"name":"payments","healthy":"Healthy"}
{"name":"payments-db","healthy":"Healthy"}
{"name":"payments-cache","healthy":"Degraded"}

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# CI/CD PIPELINE — Check deployment status after deploy
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

$ anihpj-cli deploy payments --env production --wait
🚀 Deploying payments to production...
⏳ Waiting for ArgoCD sync... (1/5)
⏳ Waiting for ArgoCD sync... (2/5) — Progressing
⏳ Waiting for ArgoCD sync... (3/5) — Progressing
✅ Deployment complete! payments is Healthy (3/3 pods)
   Endpoint: https://payments.anihpj.io

$ echo $?   # Exit code 0 = success. Non-zero = failure.
0
💡 The "Pipe-Friendly" CLI Principle

Every CLI command should follow the Unix philosophy: (1) Do one thing well. Each command has a single, clear purpose. (2) Expect text input. Commands accept pipe input where it makes sense. (3) Produce text output. Default output is human-readable. Use --output json for machine-readable. (4) Exit codes matter. Exit 0 = success. Exit non-zero = failure. CI/CD pipelines rely on exit codes to determine if a step succeeded. A CLI that always exits 0 even on failure is worse than no CLI — it silently hides production issues.

⚖️ Build vs Buy vs Assemble — How to Create Your IDP

One of the most important strategic decisions in platform engineering: Do you BUILD your IDP from scratch, BUY a commercial platform product, or ASSEMBLE it from open-source components? There's no universally correct answer — it depends on your organization's size, expertise, and needs:

AspectBUY (Commercial)ASSEMBLE (Open-Source)BUILD (From Scratch)
ExamplesHumanitec, Port, Mia-Platform, CoherenceBackstage + ArgoCD + Crossplane + Prometheus + KyvernoCustom portal + custom API + custom automation
Time to ValueDays to weeksWeeks to monthsMonths to years
CustomizationLimited — what the vendor supportsHigh — modify open-source, write pluginsMaximum — you control everything
MaintenanceVendor handles upgrades, security patchesYour team does upgrades, integration testingYour team does EVERYTHING
Cost (Year 1)$50K-$300K (licensing + setup)$150K-$400K (2-3 platform engineers)$400K-$1M+ (4-6 engineers)
Vendor Lock-in❌ High — migrating off is painful✅ Low — open standards, portable✅ None — but tied to your code
Best ForSmall/medium orgs with limited platform team, need fast resultsMedium/large orgs with 2+ platform engineers, want balance of speed + controlVery large orgs with unique requirements and 5+ platform engineers
🤔 How many dedicated platform engineers do you have?
❌ 0-1
BUY a commercial platform. You don't have the capacity to build or assemble. Get something running fast, then reassess.
✅ 2-4
ASSEMBLE from open-source (Backstage + ArgoCD + Crossplane). You have enough capacity to integrate and maintain OSS components.
✅ 5+
You CAN build from scratch... but ASSEMBLE is still recommended. Even Google and Spotify use Backstage. Building from scratch rarely pays off.
🤔 How unique are your platform requirements?
✅ Standard (CI/CD, monitoring, infra)
ASSEMBLE from OSS. 80% of your needs are solved by existing tools. Focus your custom work on the 20% that's unique to your organization.
⚠️ Highly regulated (government, defense)
BUY (with compliance certifications) or BUILD (if no vendor meets requirements). Compliance constraints may force custom solutions.
💡 The CNPA Recommendation: ASSEMBLE from Open-Source

The CNPA exam (and industry best practice) favors the ASSEMBLE approach: integrate best-of-breed open-source tools (Backstage, ArgoCD, Crossplane, Prometheus, Kyverno) into a cohesive IDP. This gives you: (1) The speed of not building everything from scratch, (2) The control of open-source (no vendor lock-in, you own the integration), (3) The community of thousands of other platform teams solving the same problems, (4) The flexibility to customize where needed through plugins and APIs. Pure BUILD is almost never the right answer. Even the largest tech companies use Backstage. Pure BUY works for smaller orgs but risks vendor lock-in as you scale.

📊 Measuring IDP Success — The Metrics That Matter

Building an IDP without measuring its impact is like driving without a dashboard. You need metrics to prove the platform's value, justify continued investment, and identify areas for improvement. These are the four key metrics every IDP should track:

🔓
1. Self-Service Rate

Definition: Percentage of infrastructure requests fulfilled by developers WITHOUT filing tickets.
Target: > 80%
How to measure: Track Backstage Scaffolder usage + CLI commands vs platform team tickets. If developers file 100 tickets/month and the portal handles 400 requests/month → 80% self-service rate.
CNPA Insight: Every ticket filed is a FAILURE of self-service. The platform's job is to make tickets unnecessary.

⏱️
2. Time-to-First-Deploy (TTFD)

Definition: Time from "I want to create a new service" to "it's deployed and healthy in production."
Target: < 15 minutes (via golden path)
How to measure: Scaffolder task creation timestamp → ArgoCD "Healthy" status timestamp.
CNPA Insight: Without an IDP, this is 2-4 DAYS (tickets, approvals, manual setup). The IDP's #1 value metric is collapsing TTFD from days to minutes.

📈
3. Platform Adoption Rate

Definition: Percentage of services running ON the platform vs total services in the organization.
Target: > 75% after 12 months
How to measure: Services in Backstage Catalog with lifecycle=production ÷ total known services.
CNPA Insight: Adoption is VOLUNTARY (golden paths are optional). If only 20% of teams use the platform, your golden paths aren't good enough. Make them better — don't mandate them.

😊
4. Developer NPS (Net Promoter Score)

Definition: "How likely are you to recommend the anihpj platform to another team?" (scale 0-10).
Target: > 50 (positive NPS)
How to measure: Quarterly survey to all developers using the platform. NPS = %Promoters (9-10) − %Detractors (0-6).
CNPA Insight: This is the ULTIMATE metric. You can have 100% adoption and still have miserable developers if the platform is forced upon them. High NPS + high adoption = you're doing it right.

80%+
Self-Service Rate
<15 min
Time-to-First-Deploy
75%+
Platform Adoption
50+
Developer NPS

💡 The Golden Rule of IDP Metrics: If you're not measuring developer satisfaction, you're not running a platform — you're running an experiment. Treat your IDP like a SaaS product. SaaS companies live and die by NPS. Your IDP should too.

🏢 Multi-Team IDP — Scaling the Platform Across 20+ Teams

A common CNPA exam scenario: your organization grows from 3 teams to 20 teams. How does the IDP scale? The answer is multi-tenancy with namespace isolation, team-scoped RBAC, and per-team golden path customization:

🏢 MULTI-TEAM IDP — One Platform, Many Teams, Perfect Isolation
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  MULTI-TEAM IDP — How the Platform Scales to 20+ Teams                │
│                                                                       │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │                   🏭 THE SHARED IDP (One Instance)                │ │
│  │                                                                  │ │
│  │  🎭 Backstage — ONE portal for ALL teams                         │ │
│  │  🚀 ArgoCD — ONE instance, watches ALL team repos               │ │
│  │  📊 Prometheus — ONE instance, scrapes ALL team metrics          │ │
│  │  🛡️ Kyverno — ONE set of cluster-wide policies                   │ │
│  │  📡 Platform API — ONE API serving ALL teams                     │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                 │                                     │
│                    ┌────────────┼────────────┐                       │
│                    ▼            ▼            ▼                       │
│  ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐    │
│  │ TEAM: payments   │ │ TEAM: shipping   │ │ TEAM: catalog    │    │
│  │ Namespace: pay-* │ │ Namespace: ship-*│ │ Namespace: cat-* │    │
│  │                  │ │                  │ │                  │    │
│  │ RBAC:            │ │ RBAC:            │ │ RBAC:            │    │
│  │ • Get/List pods  │ │ • Get/List pods  │ │ • Get/List pods  │    │
│  │   in pay-*       │ │   in ship-*      │ │   in cat-*       │    │
│  │ • Deploy to pay-*│ │ • Deploy to ship*│ │ • Deploy to cat-*│    │
│  │ • View pay-* logs│ │ • View ship-* log│ │ • View cat-* logs│    │
│  │ • CANNOT see     │ │ • CANNOT see     │ │ • CANNOT see     │    │
│  │   ship-* or cat-*│ │   pay-* or cat-* │ │   pay-* or ship-*│    │
│  │                  │ │                  │ │                  │    │
│  │ Golden Paths:    │ │ Golden Paths:    │ │ Golden Paths:    │    │
│  │ • Django Service │ │ • Django Service │ │ • Static Site    │    │
│  │ • Postgres DB    │ │ • Go Service     │ │ • CDN Config     │    │
│  │ • Redis Cache    │ │ • Kafka Topic    │ │                  │    │
│  │                  │ │                  │ │                  │    │
│  │ Resource Quota:  │ │ Resource Quota:  │ │ Resource Quota:  │    │
│  │ CPU: 16, Mem:32Gi│ │ CPU: 8, Mem:16Gi │ │ CPU: 4, Mem:8Gi  │    │
│  └──────────────────┘ └──────────────────┘ └──────────────────┘    │
│                                                                       │
│  KEY MULTI-TENANCY PRINCIPLES:                                        │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  1. NAMESPACE ISOLATION: Each team gets their own namespace(s).  │ │
│  │     Team payments can NEVER see team shipping's pods.            │ │
│  │                                                                  │ │
│  │  2. RBAC SCOPING: Each team has RoleBindings (not ClusterRoles)  │ │
│  │     scoped to their namespaces. Least privilege by default.      │ │
│  │                                                                  │ │
│  │  3. RESOURCE QUOTAS: Per-team CPU, memory, and storage limits.   │ │
│  │     Prevents one team from consuming all cluster resources.      │ │
│  │                                                                  │ │
│  │  4. NETWORK POLICIES: Default-deny between team namespaces.      │ │
│  │     Team payments CANNOT make network connections to team ship.  │ │
│  │     (Unless explicitly allowed via NetworkPolicy).                │ │
│  │                                                                  │ │
│  │  5. GOLDEN PATH CUSTOMIZATION: Different teams get DIFFERENT     │ │
│  │     golden paths based on their persona. Backend teams get       │ │
│  │     Django/Go/Postgres paths. Frontend teams get Static Site.    │ │
│  │                                                                  │ │
│  │  6. SHARED PLATFORM SERVICES: One ArgoCD instance, one           │ │
│  │     Prometheus, one Kyverno. These are CLUSTER-SCOPED services   │ │
│  │     that ALL teams benefit from. No per-team copies needed.      │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 The IDP Scales Sublinearly — Platform Team Stays Small

The magic of an IDP: as the number of development teams grows from 3 → 10 → 50, the platform team size grows from 3 → 4 → 6. This is sublinear scaling — the platform team doesn't grow proportionally with the teams it serves. This is possible because: (1) Golden paths encode expertise once and reuse it infinitely, (2) Self-service eliminates manual work per request, (3) Policy-as-code enforces standards automatically without manual review. Without an IDP, platform team size grows linearly with service count (3 → 10 → 50 engineers). With an IDP, it stays nearly flat.

21.5 Practice Lab — 10 CNPA Exam-Style Questions

Test your understanding of Internal Developer Platforms with these CNPA-exam-style multiple choice questions.

IDPs & DevEx Q1 of 10
What BEST defines an Internal Developer Platform (IDP)?
A) A single software product that you purchase and install — like a "platform-in-a-box"
B) Kubernetes with Backstage installed — that's all you need
C) An integrated ecosystem of tools (portal, automation, catalog, observability, security) that provides self-service capabilities to developers through golden paths
D) A centralized ops team that manages infrastructure for all development teams
✅ Correct Answer: C — Integrated Ecosystem

An IDP is NOT a single tool (A), NOT just K8s+Backstage (B), and definitely NOT a centralized ops team (D — that's the OPPOSITE of an IDP). An IDP is an INTEGRATED ECOSYSTEM of tools working together through a unified interface (portal + CLI + API) to provide self-service golden paths. The key word is "ecosystem" — multiple tools, integrated, working as one.

IDPs & DevEx Q2 of 10
A developer clicks "Create Django Service" in Backstage. Which of these should a COMPLETE golden path scaffold?
A) Only a GitHub repository — the developer handles the rest
B) GitHub repo + Dockerfile + K8s manifests + CI pipeline + ArgoCD Application + monitoring + catalog entry — EVERYTHING needed for production
C) A Kubernetes namespace and a blank deployment
D) Just a Backstage catalog entry — the developer provisions the rest
✅ Correct Answer: B — COMPLETE scaffold

A golden path that creates a repo and says "good luck" is NOT a golden path — it's a half-finished template. A REAL golden path scaffolds EVERYTHING: repository, CI pipeline, K8s manifests, monitoring, security policies, documentation, and catalog registration. When the path finishes, the service should be DEPLOYED and HEALTHY — not "ready for you to configure 12 more things." This is one of the most-tested CNPA concepts.

IDPs & DevEx Q3 of 10
What is the PRIMARY mechanism through which an IDP delivers value to developers?
A) Golden Paths — opinionated, pre-built workflows that scaffold complete, production-ready services
B) Documentation — comprehensive wiki pages explaining how to deploy
C) Training sessions — weekly workshops on Kubernetes and CI/CD
D) Ticket-based support — file a ticket, and the platform team provisions your infrastructure
✅ Correct Answer: A — Golden Paths

Documentation (B) is outdated the moment it's written. Training (C) doesn't scale. Ticket-based support (D) is the OLD way — the very thing the IDP exists to eliminate. Golden Paths ARE the mechanism — they encode your platform's best practices into executable workflows. Instead of DOCUMENTING how to deploy, you AUTOMATE deployment. Instead of TRAINING developers on K8s, you give them a form that generates K8s manifests automatically. Golden paths make the right way the ONLY way — not by enforcement, but by making it the easiest path.

IDPs & DevEx Q4 of 10
A golden path asks developers to choose between 5 CI tools and 4 deployment strategies. What's wrong?
A) Nothing — giving developers choice is empowering and increases adoption
B) Too many CI tools — limit it to 2 options
C) The form should have better documentation about each option
D) This is the "Choose Your Own Adventure" anti-pattern — a golden path should make ONE opinionated choice, not force developers to become platform experts
✅ Correct Answer: D — Anti-pattern

A golden path that presents 20 options is NOT simplifying anything — it's a decision tree disguised as a form. The whole point of a golden path is to make decisions FOR the developer. "We use GitHub Actions + ArgoCD. You don't choose — we chose for you, and we've tested it, secured it, and optimized it." Power users who need different tools CAN override — but the DEFAULT path should be opinionated. If developers consistently override your choice, THAT'S feedback to improve the path — not a reason to offer 5 choices.

IDPs & DevEx Q5 of 10
What is the Backstage Software Template (Scaffolder) primarily responsible for in an IDP?
A) Deploying applications to Kubernetes
B) Monitoring service health and sending alerts
C) Generating project skeletons — repository structure, Dockerfile, CI config, K8s manifests, catalog entry — from a parameterized template
D) Managing user authentication and RBAC for the platform
✅ Correct Answer: C — Project skeleton generation

The Backstage Scaffolder is a "cookie cutter" for services. It takes a template (YAML definition of what files to generate), parameters from the developer (service name, team), and produces a complete project structure. It does NOT deploy (ArgoCD does that), does NOT monitor (Prometheus does that), and does NOT handle auth (OIDC/OAuth plugins do that). The Scaffolder's job is GENERATION — turning "I want a Django service" into a GitHub repo with all the files needed for production.

IDPs & DevEx Q6 of 10
What architectural principle should a Platform CLI follow?
A) The CLI should contain all platform business logic — it's the single source of truth
B) The CLI should be a thin wrapper that calls the Platform API — all business logic lives in backend services
C) The CLI should directly call kubectl, ArgoCD APIs, and cloud provider APIs — bypassing the platform backend
D) Each development team should build their own CLI with their own conventions
✅ Correct Answer: B — Thin wrapper around Platform API

The CLI should have ZERO business logic. Every command is just an HTTP call to the Platform API. Why? (1) Consistency: The CLI and the portal call the same API — they can't diverge. (2) Simplicity: The CLI is easier to build, test, and maintain when it's just HTTP calls. (3) Security: Authentication, authorization, and rate limiting are handled by the API gateway — not by every CLI installation. (4) Future-proof: When you add a new capability to the API, both the CLI and portal get it automatically.

IDPs & DevEx Q7 of 10
A team wants to use Jenkins instead of GitHub Actions for CI. The golden path uses GitHub Actions. What should the platform team do?
A) Allow the team to override the CI step — golden paths are defaults, not prison walls. The team can use Jenkins but must integrate with the platform's deployment and monitoring APIs
B) Deny the request — all teams must use the golden path as-is for consistency
C) Immediately create a second golden path with Jenkins — every team's preference must become a golden path
D) Force the team to migrate to GitHub Actions — the platform standard is non-negotiable
✅ Correct Answer: A — Allow override with integration requirements

Golden paths are the PAVED ROAD, not prison walls. The platform team should: (1) Allow the override — the team CAN use Jenkins. (2) Define the integration contract — "You can use Jenkins, but your pipeline MUST: push images to our registry, update the K8s manifests in Git, and register with our catalog. Those are the platform's integration points." (3) Learn from the override — WHY does this team need Jenkins? Is there a feature GitHub Actions is missing? Use this as feedback to improve the golden path. CNPA principle: Golden paths are recommended, not required. Overrides are feedback.

IDPs & DevEx Q8 of 10
In the 6-layer IDP architecture, where does ArgoCD belong?
A) Portal Layer — it provides the user interface
B) Observability Layer — it monitors deployment health
C) Catalog Layer — it tracks service metadata
D) Automation Layer — it automates GitOps deployment and sync
✅ Correct Answer: D — Automation Layer

ArgoCD belongs in the Automation (Delivery) layer alongside Crossplane (infrastructure provisioning), GitHub Actions (CI execution), and the Backstage Scaffolder (template generation). The Automation layer is the "engine room" of the IDP — it's where the actual work happens. The Portal shows you WHAT'S happening. The Automation layer MAKES it happen. The Catalog layer KNOWS about it. The Observability layer WATCHES it. Each layer has a distinct responsibility.

IDPs & DevEx Q9 of 10
A new developer joins the anihpj team. Without an IDP, they need to learn 13 tools to deploy a service. With the anihpj IDP, how many tools do they ideally need to learn?
A) 10 — the IDP eliminates 3 tools
B) 7 — the most essential tools remain
C) 3 — Backstage Portal (discover + create), anihpj-cli (operate), and Git (push code)
D) 0 — the IDP handles everything, developers never touch any tools
✅ Correct Answer: C — 3 tools (77% reduction)

The goal of an IDP is to REDUCE cognitive load — not eliminate it entirely (option D is unrealistic). The ideal developer experience: (1) Backstage Portal — discover existing services, create new ones via golden paths, read TechDocs. (2) anihpj-cli — deploy, view logs, check status, get database credentials. (3) Git — push code, that's it. Everything else (Kubernetes, Docker, Terraform, Prometheus, ArgoCD, Kyverno) is ABSTRACTED behind the IDP. Developers CAN dig deeper if they want to — but they don't NEED to.

IDPs & DevEx Q10 of 10
What is the ultimate measure of IDP success — the metric that proves the platform is delivering value?
A) Number of tools integrated into the platform
B) Developer self-service rate — percentage of infrastructure tasks that developers complete WITHOUT filing tickets
C) Platform team size — a larger team means a more successful platform
D) Number of golden paths available — more paths = better platform
✅ Correct Answer: B — Self-service rate

The IDP's core purpose is SELF-SERVICE. If developers still need to file tickets for infrastructure, the IDP has failed — regardless of how many tools it integrates or how many golden paths it has. A healthy IDP should achieve >80% self-service rate: 8 out of 10 infrastructure requests are fulfilled by developers themselves through the portal, CLI, or Git-based workflows. The remaining 20% are novel scenarios that feed back into improving the golden paths. The platform's job is to make itself unnecessary — every ticket filed is a failure of self-service.

📝Scaffolder = Cookie CutterBackstage Software Templates generate complete project skeletons from parameters.

Chapter 22: API-Driven Service Catalogs

Every platform needs a brain — a central registry that knows about EVERY service, API, database, and dependency in the organization. That's the Service Catalog. It answers the questions that every developer asks daily: "Who owns this service? What depends on it? Is it healthy right now? Where's its documentation?" Without a catalog, organizations operate in the dark — developers waste hours searching for existing APIs, accidentally break dependencies, and duplicate work that already exists. The Backstage Software Catalog is the industry standard for solving this problem — and it's API-driven by design, so every piece of platform automation can query it programmatically.

⚠️ The Catalog Is the IDP's Knowledge Graph

The CNPA exam tests the Service Catalog as the DATA MODEL of your platform. Key exam patterns:

  • Entity Model — Know the Backstage entity kinds: Component (service, website, library), API, Resource (database, queue), System, Domain. Each has a specific purpose in modeling your software ecosystem.
  • catalog-info.yaml — This YAML file is the self-service registration mechanism. Developers add it to their repo and the service auto-appears in the catalog. No tickets. No manual steps.
  • Discovery vs Registration — Discovery auto-finds existing services (GitHub integration scans repos). Registration is manual (developer creates catalog-info.yaml). Both feed the same catalog.
  • Catalog as Integration Hub — Every platform tool (ArgoCD, Prometheus, PagerDuty) reads from the catalog. The catalog is the SOURCE OF TRUTH for your entire software ecosystem.

22.1 What is a Service Catalog?

A Service Catalog is the central registry of EVERYTHING in your software ecosystem. Every service. Every API. Every database. Every library. Every team. Every dependency. It answers the fundamental questions that every organization struggles with: "What services do we have? Who owns them? What do they depend on? Are they healthy? Where's the documentation?" Without a catalog, these questions are answered through tribal knowledge, Slack searches, and hallway conversations. With a catalog, they're answered instantly through a searchable, API-driven registry:

📚 The Library Analogy — Why Catalogs Are Essential Infrastructure

Think of your organization's software as a vast library. Without a catalog system, finding a book means wandering the aisles, asking librarians (who may have left), or stumbling upon things by accident. With a card catalog (or its modern equivalent, a digital search system), you find exactly what you need in seconds — including related books, the author, and where it's located. A Service Catalog is the card catalog for your software ecosystem:

📚
Library Catalog → Service Catalog

Book Title → Service Name (anihpj-api)
Author → Team Owner (team-anihpj)
Subject/Tags → Tags (django, python, rest-api)
Location on Shelf → GitHub Repo + K8s Namespace
"Also by this author" → Other services owned by the same team
"Customers who read this also..." → Dependents and depend-on relationships
Is it checked out? → Health status (Healthy/Degraded/Missing)

🤔
Without a Library Catalog

Finding a book = Asking around, searching shelves randomly ("Does anyone know where the Django API book is?")
Duplicate books = Nobody knows "Python REST APIs" already exists, so someone buys another copy (builds another payment API)
Outdated books = The "2023 Guide to Our Services" wiki is still on the shelf. Nobody removed it. New hires read it and get confused.
Unknown dependencies = "If I move this bookshelf (update this database), what books will fall?" Nobody knows until it's too late.

🔄 The Entity Lifecycle — From Creation to Retirement

Every entity in the catalog goes through a lifecycle — from the moment it's created (via a golden path or manual registration) to the moment it's retired (deprecated and removed). Understanding this lifecycle is essential for maintaining catalog hygiene:

Stage 1: Registration (Birth)

Entity enters the catalog. Either: (a) Auto-discovered via GitHub Discovery finding catalog-info.yaml, or (b) Manually registered by a developer through Backstage's "Register Existing Component" flow. Entity has lifecycle: experimental. It's visible but marked as early-stage.

Catalog Entry Created
Stage 2: Production (Adulthood)

Service graduates to production. Owner updates lifecycle: production in catalog-info.yaml. Now it shows in production dashboards, triggers PagerDuty on-call rotations, and appears in "all production services" reports. This is the steady state for most entities — they stay here for months or years.

Lifecycle Updated
Stage 3: Deprecation (Sunset Warning)

Service is being phased out. Owner updates lifecycle: deprecated. Backstage shows a prominent "⚠️ This service is deprecated" banner on the entity page. Platform tools (ArgoCD, PagerDuty) continue to function but may reduce alert sensitivity. Dependents are notified: "You depend on a deprecated service. Plan your migration."

Deprecation Notice
Stage 4: Retirement (Death)

Service is fully shut down. catalog-info.yaml is removed from the repo. GitHub Discovery detects the file is gone → removes entity from catalog on next scan. All platform tool integrations are automatically cleaned up: ArgoCD stops tracking it, PagerDuty removes the escalation, Grafana archives the dashboard. The entity's knowledge graph connections (dependsOn, providesApis) are severed — dependents are now "orphaned" until they update their own catalog-info.yaml.

Entity Removed
📖 Catalog Hygiene: Why Lifecycle Management Matters

A catalog that never removes dead services becomes UNTRUSTWORTHY. Developers search for "payment API" and find 4 results — 1 is production, 1 is experimental (abandoned), 2 are deprecated but still listed. They don't know which one to use. They build a FIFTH payment API. Catalog hygiene means: (1) Every entity has an accurate lifecycle field, (2) Deprecated services are eventually removed, (3) "Last deployed" dates help identify zombie services (last deployed > 180 days ago → investigate). The CNPA exam tests your awareness that the catalog must be MAINTAINED, not just created. A stale catalog is worse than no catalog — it's actively misleading.

🗺️ The GPS Navigation Analogy — How the Catalog Guides Every Decision

Think of your software ecosystem as a vast city. Without a GPS (the catalog), navigating means asking strangers for directions, following outdated paper maps, and hoping you don't hit dead ends. With a GPS, you know exactly where you are, where everything else is, what routes connect them, and — crucially — whether there's traffic ahead (a service is degraded):

🗺️
GPS Navigation → Service Catalog

Current Location → Your service in the catalog
Destination → The API you need to call
Route → The dependency chain (dependsOn → providesApis)
Traffic Alert → Degraded status ("⚠️ Route congested" = "⚠️ Service degraded")
Road Closure → Deprecated lifecycle ("🚧 Road closed ahead" = "🚧 Service deprecated")
Estimated Time → "Last deployed 3 hours ago" = service is actively maintained
Map Updates → GitHub Discovery auto-refreshes the catalog every 30 minutes — the map is always current

📊
The Cost of No Catalog — Real Numbers

Developer Discovery Time: 2-4 hours per week searching for existing services, APIs, and owners. 50 developers = 100-200 hours/week LOST.
Duplicate Services: Without a catalog, teams build services that already exist. ~5% of services are unnecessary duplicates. At $50K/service/year, 100 services = $250K/year wasted on duplicates.
Incidents from Unknown Dependencies: 30% of production incidents involve unexpected dependency breakage. Average incident cost: $5K. 12 incidents/year = $60K/year.
Onboarding Time: New developers spend 2-3 weeks just learning "what services exist." Catalog reduces this to 1-2 days. At $150K/developer salary, this saves $30K per new hire.

🚨 The Catalog During Incidents — From Panic to Precision

The catalog's value is never more apparent than during a production incident. Without a catalog, incident response is chaotic: "What services depend on the failing database? Who owns them? Who's on call? Where are the runbooks?" With a catalog, every answer is one click away:

❌ INCIDENT WITHOUT CATALOG (The Panic Model)

3:00 AM: PagerDuty fires: "anihpj-db connection failures."

3:02 AM: On-call engineer: "What services use this database?!" → Searches Slack. "Anyone know what depends on anihpj-db?" No response (it's 3 AM).

3:15 AM: Checks old architecture diagram. It's from 2024. Lists 3 dependents. Actually there are 7 — 4 were added since the diagram was last updated.

3:30 AM: 4 services are now crashing because they can't connect to the database. On-call pages 4 more teams. Chaos escalates.

MTTR: 90+ minutes. Teams paged: 5. Services affected: 7. Root cause found: at 4:15 AM.

✅ INCIDENT WITH CATALOG (The Precision Model)

3:00 AM: PagerDuty fires: "anihpj-db connection failures."

3:01 AM: On-call opens Backstage. Searches "anihpj-db." Clicks "Dependents." Catalog shows: anihpj-api, anihpj-web, payment-api, shipping-svc, invoice-svc, auth-svc, reporting-svc. All 7 dependents listed with owners and on-call contacts.

3:03 AM: PagerDuty plugin shows on-call for each dependent team. On-call notifies all 4 team rotations simultaneously.

3:05 AM: Each team checks their service: 3 are already auto-failing over to read replicas. 4 need manual intervention. On-call coordinates via Slack channel auto-created from catalog team data.

MTTR: 22 minutes. Teams paged: 4 (only affected). Services affected: 7 (all known before impact). Root cause: database connection pool exhausted — fixed at 3:15 AM.

💡 The Catalog Turns Unknown-Unknowns into Known-Knowns

Before a catalog, "what depends on this database?" is an unknown-unknown — you don't know what you don't know, and you can't act until it's too late. After a catalog, it becomes a known-known — you can query it BEFORE making changes, BEFORE incidents happen. This shift from reactive discovery ("what broke?") to proactive planning ("what WILL break if I do this?") is the catalog's greatest contribution to operational excellence. The CNPA exam will present incident scenarios and ask how the catalog improves response. The answer always involves: faster dependency discovery, automatic owner identification, and integration with incident management tools.

🧠 The Catalog as a Knowledge Graph — Not Just a List

A service catalog isn't a flat list of services — it's a knowledge graph. Entities (services, APIs, databases, teams) are connected through relationships (dependsOn, providesApis, ownedBy). This graph structure enables powerful queries that flat registries can't answer: "What services will be affected if I take this database offline for maintenance?" "Which teams own services that haven't been deployed in 30 days?" "Show me all services that depend on this deprecated API.":

📦 Catalog
🐍
Components

Services, websites, libraries — the things you BUILD

What you own
🔗
APIs

REST, GraphQL, gRPC endpoints — how services communicate

How they connect
🗄️
Resources

Databases, queues, caches — infrastructure dependencies

What they depend on
👥
Systems

Logical grouping of related components (e.g., "Payment System")

How they're grouped
🌐
Domains

Business areas (e.g., "Payments Domain", "Shipping Domain")

Business context
👤
Teams & Users

Who owns what — the organizational mapping

Accountability

🐍 Before vs After Catalog — The anihpj Developer Experience

❌ WITHOUT A SERVICE CATALOG

Developer: "Is there already a payment API?"
→ Searches Slack. Finds a thread from 2024. "Bob built one." Bob left last year. No docs.
→ Builds a NEW payment API. Now there are TWO.

Developer: "I need to update the database schema. What depends on it?"
→ Nobody knows. Deploys on Friday at 5 PM. 4 services break. Rollback. Incident.

New Developer: "What services does our team own?"
→ Team lead: "Check the wiki." Wiki is from 2023. Lists 5 services. Actually there are 12. 7 are undocumented. 2 are abandoned.

✅ WITH A SERVICE CATALOG

Developer: "Is there already a payment API?"
→ Opens Backstage. Searches "payment". Finds: 💳 payment-api | Owner: payments-team | Status: ✅ Healthy. Does NOT build a duplicate.

Developer: "I need to update the database. What depends on it?"
→ Opens anihpj-db entity. Clicks "Dependents." Catalog shows: anihpj-api, anihpj-web, payment-api. Coordinates BEFORE deploying. Zero breakage.

New Developer: "What services does our team own?"
→ Opens team-anihpj entity. All 8 services listed. Health status for each. Docs linked. 2 flagged: "Last deployed: 180 days ago → Consider deprecation."

📈 The Catalog Maturity Model — From Chaos to Knowledge Graph

🗣️
LEVEL 1
Tribal Knowledge

"Ask Bob." Bob left. Nobody knows what services exist or who owns them. Slack searches are the primary discovery mechanism.

Discovery: HOURS
📝
LEVEL 2
Wiki/Confluence

A wiki page lists services. Updated manually. Always out of date. Services created last week aren't listed. Deleted services still show.

Discovery: 10-30 min
📦
LEVEL 3
Automated Catalog ⬅ CNPA

Backstage Catalog. Auto-discovered from Git. Always up-to-date because it mirrors Git. Searchable. Relationships mapped. Programmable via API.

Discovery: 5 SECONDS
🧠
LEVEL 4
AI-Enhanced

AI analyzes dependencies, suggests ownership, detects abandoned services, predicts impact of changes before deployment.

Discovery: INSTANT

💡 Why the Catalog Must Be API-Driven

The catalog isn't just a UI — it's a programmable knowledge base. Every piece of platform automation queries the catalog API. This is the "API-driven" in "API-Driven Service Catalogs" — and it's what makes the catalog the integration hub of your IDP:

Shell — How Platform Tools Query the Catalog API Programmatically 
# ─── ArgoCD plugin: "Show me all components owned by team-anihpj" ───
curl -s https://backstage.anihpj.io/api/catalog/entities \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -d '{"filter": {"kind": "Component", "spec.owner": "team-anihpj"}}' \
  | jq '.items[].metadata.name'

# ─── Impact analysis: "What depends on anihpj-db?" ───
curl -s https://backstage.anihpj.io/api/catalog/entities/by-name/resource/default/anihpj-db \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  | jq '.relations[] | select(.type=="dependentOf") | .target.name'

# ─── CI/CD pipeline: "Is this service registered? If not, auto-register it." ───
if ! curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" \
  "https://backstage.anihpj.io/api/catalog/entities/by-name/component/default/$SVC" \
  | grep -q 200; then
  echo "Service not in catalog — auto-registering..."
fi

# ─── Grafana plugin: "Find all dashboards for services in the payments system" ───
curl -s https://backstage.anihpj.io/api/catalog/entities \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -d '{"filter": {"kind": "Component", "spec.system": "jobpost"}}' \
  | jq -r '.items[].metadata.annotations["grafana/dashboard-selector"]'

22.2 The Backstage Software Catalog — Entity Model & YAML Format

The Backstage Software Catalog is the industry standard for service catalogs. It models your entire software ecosystem as entities described in YAML files. Every entity follows a standard structure — and once you understand the model, you can describe ANYTHING: services, APIs, databases, teams, and more:

📋 The core entity — catalog-info.yaml for the anihpj application stack

📋 ANIHPJ APPLICATION STACK — Modeled in the Backstage Catalog

📋 The Entity Anatomy — How Backstage Models Everything

Every entity in the Backstage catalog follows the same fundamental structure. Once you understand this anatomy, you can model anything:

🔍 Backstage Entity Anatomy

🏷️ apiVersion
backstage.io/v1alpha1 — The Backstage API version. Currently v1alpha1. As Backstage stabilizes, this will advance to v1beta1 → v1.
📦 kind
What TYPE of entity: Component (service, website, library), API (REST, GraphQL, gRPC), Resource (database, queue, cache), System (logical grouping), Domain (business area), Group (team), User (person). Each kind has a specific purpose.
📝 metadata
name (unique identifier), description, tags, annotations (key-value pairs for integrations), links (URLs for docs, dashboards). Annotations are how Backstage plugins discover entities — e.g., github.com/project-slug tells the GitHub plugin which repo to pull data from.
⚙️ spec
type (what kind of component: service, website, library), lifecycle (experimental, production, deprecated), owner (which team), system (which system it belongs to), dependsOn (what it needs), providesApis (what APIs it exposes). The spec is the "guts" that define relationships.

� Modeling Your Organization — Teams, Users, and Business Domains

The catalog doesn't just model software — it models the people and organization around the software. When you declare spec.owner: team-anihpj, Backstage looks up that team in the catalog and creates an ownedBy relationship. This enables "team views" — a dashboard showing everything a team owns, their on-call rotations, and their operational health. Here's how to model your organization:

YAML — Modeling Teams, Users, and Domains in the Catalog 
# ═══════════ GROUP: team-anihpj (The Team Entity) ═══════════
# This is what spec.owner: team-anihpj resolves to
apiVersion: backstage.io/v1alpha1
kind: Group
metadata:
  name: team-anihpj
  description: The anihpj platform team — owns the JobPost application
spec:
  type: team
  profile:
    displayName: Anihpj Platform Team
    email: platform@anihpj.io
    picture: https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/anihpj-team
  parent: platform-engineering     # This team reports to platform-eng dept
  children: []                      # No sub-teams
  members:
    - user:alice                   # References User entities
    - user:bob
    - user:charlie

# ═══════════ USER: alice (Individual Person) ═══════════
apiVersion: backstage.io/v1alpha1
kind: User
metadata:
  name: alice
spec:
  profile:
    displayName: Alice Chen
    email: alice@anihpj.io
    picture: https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/alice
  memberOf:
    - team-anihpj                   # Alice belongs to this team
    - platform-oncall               # Alice is also in the on-call rotation

# ═══════════ DOMAIN: job-board (Business Area) ═══════════
# Groups MULTIPLE systems under one business domain
apiVersion: backstage.io/v1alpha1
kind: Domain
metadata:
  name: job-board
  description: Job posting, search, and application management
spec:
  owner: platform-engineering

# ═══════════ SYSTEM: jobpost (now linked to the domain) ═══════════
apiVersion: backstage.io/v1alpha1
kind: System
metadata:
  name: jobpost
  description: Anihpj JobPost application suite
spec:
  owner: team-anihpj
  domain: job-board                # ← Links system to business domain

# ═══════════ COMPONENT: anihpj-api (belongs to team + system) ═══════════
apiVersion: backstage.io/v1alpha1
kind: Component
metadata:
  name: anihpj-api
spec:
  type: service
  lifecycle: production
  owner: team-anihpj               # ← Resolves to Group entity above
  system: jobpost                   # ← Resolves to System entity above
📖 The Organizational Hierarchy in Backstage

Backstage models your organization as a tree: Domain (business area like "Payments") → System (logical grouping like "Payment Processing") → Component/Resource (the actual software). Group (team) and User (person) are separate from this hierarchy — they connect via spec.owner. This separation is intentional: software hierarchy and organizational hierarchy are DIFFERENT things. A team can own components across multiple systems. A component can change owners without changing systems. The catalog models BOTH independently and connects them through relationships.

�🔗 Entity Relationships — How the Knowledge Graph Connects Everything

The catalog's real power isn't listing entities — it's modeling relationships between them. When you write dependsOn: [resource:anihpj-db], you're not just adding a text label — you're creating a directed graph edge that enables queries like "show me everything that breaks if I take this database offline." Understanding the relationship types is essential because they're what transform the catalog from a flat list into a knowledge graph:

RelationshipDirectionExampleWhat It Enables
dependsOnComponent → Resource/Componentanihpj-api → dependsOn → anihpj-db"What does this service NEED to function?" Impact analysis: "anihpj-db is going down for maintenance — which services are affected?"
providesApisComponent → APIanihpj-api → providesApis → anihpj-api (the API entity)"What APIs does this service expose?" API consumers can find the API definition (OpenAPI spec) linked from here.
consumesApisComponent → APIanihpj-web → consumesApis → anihpj-api"What APIs does this service CALL?" The reverse of providesApis. Shows the API consumer side of the relationship.
ownedByEntity → Group (Team)anihpj-api → ownedBy → team-anihpjSet via spec.owner. "Who is responsible for this service?" Enables team-based views: "Show me everything owned by payments-team."
partOfEntity → System/Domainanihpj-api → partOf → jobpost (System)Set via spec.system. "Which system does this belong to?" Enables system views: "Show me everything in the JobPost system."
hasPartSystem → Entityjobpost → hasPart → anihpj-apiThe reverse of partOf. Auto-derived by Backstage. "What components make up this system?"
💡 The Catalog Is a DIRECTED GRAPH — Not a Flat List

This is the single most important concept for the CNPA exam. The catalog is a directed graph, not a database table. Entities are NODES. Relationships are DIRECTED EDGES. This means you can traverse the graph in ANY direction: "Show me everything that depends on this database" (reverse traversal of dependsOn). "Show me the system that contains this component" (traverse partOf upward). "Show me all APIs in the payments domain" (traverse partOf → hasPart → providesApis). If you understand the catalog as a graph, you understand why it's so powerful. If you think of it as a flat list, you'll miss 90% of its value.

⚙️ Catalog Processors — How Backstage Enriches Raw Entities

When Backstage ingests a catalog-info.yaml file, it doesn't just store it as-is. It runs the entity through a pipeline of processors — each processor adds, validates, or transforms data. Understanding this pipeline is essential for debugging catalog issues and for building custom catalog integrations:

⚙️ CATALOG PROCESSORS — The Enrichment Pipeline
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  CATALOG PROCESSORS — How Raw YAML Becomes a Rich Entity              │

│  RAW YAML (catalog-info.yaml):                                        │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  apiVersion: backstage.io/v1alpha1                               │ │
│  │  kind: Component                                                 │ │

│  │    type: service                                                 │ │
│  │    lifecycle: production                                         │ │

│  │    dependsOn: [resource:anihpj-db]                              │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                         │                                             │
│                         ▼                                             │
│  PROCESSOR PIPELINE (sequential, each adds something):                │
│                                                                       │

│  │  1. PLACEHOLDER RESOLVER                                         │ │
│  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ │

│  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │ │
│  │                                                                  │ │
│  │  2. URL READER                                                   │ │
│  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ │
│  │  │  If spec contains a URL reference (e.g., GitHub URL to      │ │ │
│  │  │  OpenAPI spec), fetches and caches the content.             │ │ │
│  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │ │
│  │                                                                  │ │
│  │  3. ANNOTATION PROCESSORS (Plugin-Specific)                      │ │
│  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ │
│  │  │  github.com/project-slug → GitHub processor enriches entity │ │ │
│  │  │    with repo metadata: language, default branch, README    │ │ │
│  │  │  pagerduty.com/service-id → PagerDuty processor enriches   │ │ │

│  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │ │
│  │                                                                  │ │
│  │  4. RELATION PROCESSORS                                          │ │
│  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ │
│  │  │  dependsOn, providesApis, consumesApis → creates graph      │ │ │

│  │  │  spec.owner → creates ownedBy edge to Group entity          │ │ │
│  │  │  spec.system → creates partOf edge to System entity         │ │ │

│                         ▼                                             │

│  • Graph edges to owner team, system, dependencies created            │
│  • Reverse edges (hasPart, dependencyOf) auto-computed               │

22.3 Catalog Discovery — Auto-Discovering Your Software Ecosystem

Manually registering every service in the catalog doesn't scale. Catalog Discovery is Backstage's mechanism for automatically finding and registering services from your existing infrastructure. Instead of "create a catalog entry for every repo," you point Backstage at your GitHub organization and it scans for catalog-info.yaml files — automatically registering every service it finds:

🔍 CATALOG DISCOVERY — How Backstage Auto-Finds Services
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  CATALOG DISCOVERY — Automatic Service Registration                   │
│                                                                       │
│  DISCOVERY METHODS (How Backstage Finds Services):                     │
│                                                                       │
│  METHOD 1: GitHub Discovery (Most Common)                              │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  app-config.yaml:                                                │ │
│  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ │
│  │  │  catalog:                                                   │ │ │
│  │  │    locations:                                               │ │ │
│  │  │      - type: github-discovery                              │ │ │
│  │  │        target: https://github.com/anihpj                    │ │ │
│  │  │  # Backstage scans EVERY repo in the anihpj GitHub org      │ │ │
│  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │ │
│  │                                                                  │ │
│  │  How it works:                                                   │ │
│  │  1. Backstage queries GitHub API: "List all repos in anihpj org"│ │
│  │  2. For each repo, check for catalog-info.yaml in:               │ │
│  │     • /catalog-info.yaml (repo root)                            │ │
│  │     • /.backstage/catalog-info.yaml (Backstage directory)       │ │
│  │  3. If found → Parse the YAML → Register entity in catalog      │ │
│  │  4. If NOT found → Skip this repo (no catalog entry)            │ │
│  │  5. Re-scan every 30 minutes (configurable)                     │ │
│  │                                                                  │ │
│  │  Result: 0 manual registration. Push catalog-info.yaml to a     │ │
│  │  new repo → within 30 minutes, it auto-appears in the catalog.  │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                       │
│  METHOD 2: URL-Based Location (For External Sources)                   │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │

│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                       │

│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │

⚙️ The Catalog Ingestion Pipeline — From YAML to Knowledge Graph

Behind the scenes, Backstage's catalog ingestion is a multi-stage pipeline. Understanding this pipeline helps you debug "why isn't my service showing up in the catalog?" problems:

1
Fetch

Catalog reads locations from app-config. GitHub Discovery queries the API for repos.

2
Read

For each location, read the YAML file(s). Parse into raw entity objects.

3
Validate

Each entity is validated against its kind's schema. Invalid entities are rejected with an error.

4
Enrich

Processors add computed fields: default lifecycle, tag normalization, annotation processing.

5
Store

Valid entities are stored in the catalog database (SQLite or PostgreSQL). Now searchable!

💡 Common failure point: Step 3 (Validation). If your catalog-info.yaml has a typo in apiVersion or uses an unsupported kind, the entity is silently rejected. Check Backstage logs: kubectl logs -l app=backstage | grep "Failed to process".

🔧 Troubleshooting Discovery — "Why Isn't My Service Showing Up?"

This is the #1 catalog support question. Here's a systematic debugging checklist for when a service doesn't appear in the Backstage catalog:

❌ Symptom: Service not appearing in catalog after pushing catalog-info.yaml
  • Check 1: Did you wait long enough? GitHub Discovery scans every 30 minutes by default. If you just pushed 2 minutes ago, it hasn't scanned yet. Wait 30 minutes or manually trigger a scan in Backstage settings.
  • Check 2: Is catalog-info.yaml in the RIGHT location? Backstage looks in: /catalog-info.yaml (repo root) and /.backstage/catalog-info.yaml (Backstage directory). If your file is in /docs/catalog-info.yaml, it won't be found.
  • Check 3: Is the YAML valid? A YAML syntax error causes silent rejection. Validate with: yamllint catalog-info.yaml or paste into an online YAML validator. Common errors: tabs instead of spaces, missing quotes around values with special characters.
  • Check 4: Does the entity pass schema validation? Check Backstage logs for validation errors. Common errors: apiVersion typo (backstage.io/v1alpha1 not backstage.io/v1alpha), unsupported kind, missing required field like spec.owner.
  • Check 5: Is GitHub Discovery configured correctly? Verify your GitHub org name in app-config.yaml matches exactly. Backstage must have a GitHub token with repo read permissions.
  • Check 6: Are there naming conflicts? Two entities with the same metadata.name and kind conflict. The second one is rejected. Check for duplicate names across repos.

📈 Scaling Catalog Discovery — Multi-Source Strategies for Large Organizations

As your organization grows, a single GitHub org scan may not be enough. Large enterprises often have services across multiple GitHub organizations, GitLab instances, Bitbucket, and even manually maintained registries. Backstage supports combining MULTIPLE discovery sources into one unified catalog:

📈 MULTI-SOURCE DISCOVERY — One Catalog, Many Data Sources
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  SCALING CATALOG DISCOVERY — Multiple Sources, One Unified View        │
│                                                                       │
│  app-config.yaml — Combine Multiple Discovery Sources:                 │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  catalog:                                                        │ │
│  │    locations:                                                    │ │
│  │      # Source 1: Main GitHub org (500+ repos)                    │ │
│  │      - type: github-discovery                                   │ │
│  │        target: https://github.com/anihpj                         │ │
│  │                                                                  │ │
│  │      # Source 2: Acquired company's GitHub org (legacy services) │ │
│  │      - type: github-discovery                                   │ │
│  │        target: https://github.com/acquired-startup               │ │
│  │                                                                  │ │
│  │      # Source 3: GitLab instance (some teams use GitLab)         │ │
│  │      - type: gitlab-discovery                                   │ │
│  │        target: https://gitlab.internal.anihpj.io                 │ │
│  │                                                                  │ │
│  │      # Source 4: Centralized catalog file (manually maintained)  │ │
│  │      - type: url                                                │ │
│  │        target: https://docs.anihpj.io/catalog/all-services.yaml │ │
│  │        rules:                                                    │ │

22.4 Catalog-Driven Development — The Catalog as Integration Hub

The catalog isn't just a directory — it's the integration hub of your entire platform. When a service is registered in the catalog, it triggers a cascade of automated setup across every platform tool. This is "catalog-driven development" — the catalog entry is the single action that provisions everything else:

📋 Catalog Annotations — The Glue That Connects Everything

Annotations are key-value pairs in entity metadata that tell Backstage plugins HOW to connect to external tools. Every plugin reads specific annotations — and adding them is how you "wire up" a service to the platform:

PluginAnnotationWhat It Does
GitHubgithub.com/project-slug: anihpj/paymentsShows repo info, README, contributors, language stats
ArgoCDargocd/app-name: paymentsShows deployment status, sync state, health
Prometheusprometheus.io/rule: payments-alertsShows alerts and metrics for this service
Grafanagrafana/dashboard-selector: "service=payments"Embeds the service's Grafana dashboard on entity page
PagerDutypagerduty.com/service-id: P123ABCShows on-call engineer, escalation policy
Sentrysentry.io/project-slug: anihpj/paymentsShows error tracking, crash reports
TechDocsbackstage.io/techdocs-ref: dir:.Builds documentation from the repo's /docs folder
SonarQubesonarqube.org/project-key: anihpj-paymentsShows code quality metrics, technical debt

💡 The CNPA Insight: Annotations are the "wiring" of your platform. When a golden path scaffolds a new service, it automatically adds the correct annotations to catalog-info.yaml. Developers never manually configure these — the template handles it. This is how the IDP achieves "built-in, not bolted-on" observability and integrations.

22.5 Practice Lab — 10 CNPA Exam-Style Questions

Test your understanding of API-Driven Service Catalogs with these CNPA-exam-style questions.

IDPs & DevEx Q1 of 10
What is the PRIMARY purpose of a Service Catalog in an Internal Developer Platform?
A) To replace Kubernetes — the catalog manages deployments directly
B) To serve as the central registry of ALL services, APIs, resources, and their relationships — answering "who owns what, what depends on what, is it healthy?"
C) To provide a graphical dashboard for Kubernetes pod metrics
D) To store application source code in a centralized repository
✅ Correct Answer: B — Central registry of the software ecosystem

The catalog is the "brain" of the IDP. It doesn't replace K8s (A), it's not just a dashboard (C), and it doesn't store source code (D). It models the RELATIONSHIPS between all software entities — services, APIs, databases, teams, systems, and domains. It answers the fundamental questions: who owns this? what depends on it? is it healthy? where's the documentation?

IDPs & DevEx Q2 of 10
In Backstage's entity model, which kind should a PostgreSQL database be registered as?
A) Component — type: service
B) API — type: grpc
C) System
D) Resource — type: database
✅ Correct Answer: D — Resource, type: database

Databases, caches, queues, and other infrastructure dependencies are modeled as Resource entities. A Component (A) is for things you BUILD (services, websites, libraries). An API (B) is for API definitions (REST, GraphQL, gRPC endpoints). A System (C) groups related components and resources. The correct model: Component (service) → dependsOn → Resource (database).

IDPs & DevEx Q3 of 10
How does Backstage's GitHub Discovery auto-register services?
A) It scans all repos in the GitHub org for catalog-info.yaml files — any repo with this file is auto-registered in the catalog
B) It reads the package.json of every repo and infers service metadata
C) It requires developers to manually submit each service for registration via a form
D) It automatically registers every repo regardless of content
✅ Correct Answer: A — Scans repos for catalog-info.yaml

GitHub Discovery queries the GitHub API to list all repos in an organization. For each repo, it checks for catalog-info.yaml. If found → parse and register. If not found → skip. This is the "self-service registration" model: developers add catalog-info.yaml to their repo, and within 30 minutes (configurable scan interval), the service auto-appears in the Backstage catalog. No tickets. No manual steps.

IDPs & DevEx Q4 of 10
What is "Catalog-Driven Development"?
A) Developers write catalog entries instead of application code
B) The catalog automatically generates application code from YAML definitions
C) A single catalog-info.yaml registration triggers automated setup across ALL platform tools — ArgoCD, Prometheus, PagerDuty, TechDocs are all wired up automatically from the catalog entry
D) Developers manually configure each platform tool after registering in the catalog
✅ Correct Answer: C — One catalog entry triggers all platform integrations

"Catalog-Driven Development" means the catalog entry IS the integration mechanism. When a service is registered with the right annotations, EVERY platform plugin automatically connects: ArgoCD shows deployment status, Prometheus shows metrics, PagerDuty shows on-call, TechDocs builds documentation, GitHub shows repo info. The catalog entry is the SINGLE ACTION that provisions all platform integrations. No manual configuration per tool.

IDPs & DevEx Q5 of 10
What are Backstage catalog annotations primarily used for?
A) Storing application configuration values like database connection strings
B) Providing key-value metadata that Backstage PLUGINS read to connect entities to external tools — e.g., github.com/project-slug tells the GitHub plugin which repo to query
C) Defining the visual appearance of the entity in the Backstage UI (colors, icons)
D) Storing encrypted secrets for the service to use at runtime
✅ Correct Answer: B — Plugin integration metadata

Annotations are how plugins "find" their external counterparts. github.com/project-slug → GitHub plugin knows which repo to query. argocd/app-name → ArgoCD plugin knows which application to show. pagerduty.com/service-id → PagerDuty plugin knows which on-call rotation to display. Annotations are NOT for application config (A — that's ConfigMaps), NOT for UI theming (C), and NOT for secrets (D — that's Kubernetes Secrets or External Secrets Operator).

IDPs & DevEx Q6 of 10
A service's catalog-info.yaml has dependsOn: [resource:anihpj-db]. What does this enable?
A) The catalog automatically creates the database if it doesn't exist
B) The catalog blocks deployment until the database is healthy
C) The catalog copies database credentials to the service
D) Impact analysis — you can query "what services depend on anihpj-db?" and the catalog shows all dependents. If you plan to update the database, you know exactly which services will be affected
✅ Correct Answer: D — Enables impact analysis queries

dependsOn builds the catalog's KNOWLEDGE GRAPH. It doesn't provision resources (A — that's Crossplane), doesn't block deployments (B — that's Kyverno or ArgoCD), and doesn't copy credentials (C — that's External Secrets Operator). What it DOES: enables queries like "show me all services that depend on anihpj-db." Before updating the database schema, you run this query and know EXACTLY which services to coordinate with. This is the catalog's superpower — turning unknown dependencies into known, queryable relationships.

IDPs & DevEx Q7 of 10
A developer pushes a new repo WITHOUT catalog-info.yaml. What happens in Backstage?
A) Nothing — GitHub Discovery skips repos without catalog-info.yaml. The service does NOT appear in the catalog
B) Backstage creates a default catalog-info.yaml automatically for every new repo
C) Backstage sends an alert to the platform team to manually register the service
D) The repo appears in the catalog with "unknown" metadata
✅ Correct Answer: A — Service does NOT appear in catalog

GitHub Discovery ONLY registers repos that contain catalog-info.yaml. This is by design — the catalog-info.yaml file is the developer's explicit declaration: "I want this service in the catalog." If a repo doesn't have one, Backstage assumes the developer hasn't opted in yet. This is why golden paths (Chapter 21's Scaffolder) automatically generate catalog-info.yaml for every new service — so services are catalog-ready from day one. For existing services without catalog-info.yaml, developers add it manually — a one-time 5-minute task.

IDPs & DevEx Q8 of 10
What Backstage entity kind would you use to group the anihpj-web, anihpj-api, and anihpj-db entities together?
A) Component — type: service
B) Domain
C) System
D) Group
✅ Correct Answer: C — System

A System groups related components and resources that work together. "JobPost" is a system — it contains anihpj-web (website), anihpj-api (service), anihpj-db (database), and anihpj-redis (cache). A Domain (B) is a higher-level grouping of systems by business area (e.g., "Payments Domain" contains multiple systems). A Group (D) represents a team or organizational unit — not a software grouping. The hierarchy is: Domain → System → Component/Resource.

IDPs & DevEx Q9 of 10
What happens in the Backstage catalog ingestion pipeline when an entity fails validation?
A) The entity is registered with a "warning" status — it still appears in the catalog but with a validation error badge
B) The entity is REJECTED silently — it does NOT appear in the catalog. The error is logged in Backstage's server logs
C) Backstage sends an email to the entity owner asking them to fix the validation error
D) Backstage auto-corrects common validation errors and registers the corrected entity
✅ Correct Answer: B — Rejected silently, error in server logs

The catalog ingestion pipeline rejects invalid entities at the Validation stage. The entity does NOT appear in the catalog. The error is logged in Backstage's server logs — not surfaced to the developer in the UI. This is a common source of confusion: "I pushed catalog-info.yaml, why isn't my service showing up?" The fix: check Backstage logs for validation errors, fix the YAML, push again. Common validation errors: typo in apiVersion, unsupported kind, missing required spec fields (like owner), invalid lifecycle value.

IDPs & DevEx Q10 of 10
What is the IDEAL state for catalog registration in a mature platform?
A) 100% manual registration — every service is carefully reviewed before appearing in the catalog
B) 50% auto-discovered, 50% manually registered — balanced approach
C) No catalog at all — developers use Slack and wikis to find services
D) 100% automated — every service has catalog-info.yaml generated by golden paths, auto-discovered via GitHub Discovery, 0% manual registration
✅ Correct Answer: D — 100% automated, 0% manual

The catalog should be COMPLETELY automated. Golden paths (Backstage Scaffolder) auto-generate catalog-info.yaml for every new service. GitHub Discovery auto-registers them. Existing services without catalog-info.yaml are migrated — a one-time manual addition, then auto-discovered forever after. The catalog becomes a TRUE reflection of what's in Git — no manual upkeep needed. This is the platform engineering ideal: the catalog is always up-to-date because it's driven by automation, not human effort.

🏷️ Backstage Entity Kinds — The 4 Fundamental Types

Every item in the Backstage catalog has an entity kind. These 4 kinds model your entire software ecosystem:

📦 Component — A piece of software (service, website, library, CLI) 🔌 API — A defined interface (REST, gRPC, GraphQL, AsyncAPI) 🗄️ Resource — Infrastructure dependency (database, queue, cache, bucket) 🌐 System — A collection of components that form a logical unit 👥 Domain — Organizational grouping (team, business unit, department)

💡 CNPA Pattern: Every service gets a Component. Every database gets a Resource. Every team gets a Domain. Relationships (dependsOn, providesApi, partOf) connect them into a living knowledge graph.

Chapter 23: Developer Portals — Backstage

Every platform capability we've built — Kubernetes, ArgoCD, Prometheus, Crossplane, Kyverno — is powerful. But power without accessibility is useless. The Developer Portal is the unified frontend that makes ALL of these capabilities accessible to developers through a single, intuitive interface. That portal is Backstage — Spotify's open-source developer portal, donated to the CNCF in 2020, and now the industry standard for Internal Developer Platforms. Instead of developers navigating 13 different UIs (K8s dashboard, ArgoCD UI, Grafana, PagerDuty, GitHub, etc.), Backstage brings everything into ONE place — with search, documentation, service creation, and deep integrations. This chapter explores what Backstage is, how its architecture works, the plugin ecosystem that makes it extensible, and how it drives platform adoption through superior developer experience.
